m1-l1.html:
What you'll learn

  • Open a new Arduino Uno project in Wokwi, with or without an account.
  • Find the code editor, the parts menu, the play button, and the Serial Monitor.
  • Name the Uno's digital, PWM, analog, and power pins.
  • Know which optional parts are worth buying, and which you can skip.

Every circuit in this course runs on a board that costs nothing: a simulated Arduino Uno inside your browser. You can wire an LED backwards, forget a resistor, or connect the wrong pin, and nothing gets hot or breaks. When you are ready for real parts, the same code runs unchanged on a real Uno.

The simulator is Wokwi (wokwi.com). It needs no install and no payment, and you can run circuits without signing in. A free account only matters when you want Wokwi to save projects for you.

#What you need, and what is optional

You need a computer with a recent web browser (Chrome, Edge, Firefox, or Safari) and an internet connection. Windows, macOS, ChromeOS, and Linux all work, because everything happens in the browser. A tablet can open Wokwi too, but drawing wires with a finger is slow, so use a mouse or trackpad if you can.

Hardware is optional for every lesson. If you want to build for real later, these are the parts that match the course:

Optional part What it is for When it helps
Arduino Uno starter kit A Uno (or compatible board), USB cable, breadboard, LEDs, resistors, buttons, a potentiometer Modules 2 to 4
Extra sensors Light, temperature, distance, and soil moisture sensors Module 4 onward
2WD robot chassis kit A small chassis with two DC motors and wheels; most kits also need a motor driver board and a AA battery pack The robot modules and the capstone

💡 Tip

Don't buy anything yet. Finish Module 4 in the simulator first. By then you will know exactly which parts you want, and you will be able to read the parts list in a kit description.

#Open your first Wokwi project

  1. Go to wokwi.com.
  2. Under Simulate with Wokwi Online, click the Arduino (Uno, Mega, Nano) tile.
  3. Scroll to Start from Scratch and click Arduino Uno.

A new project opens with a code editor on one side and a drawing of an Arduino Uno on the other. You can also bookmark the direct link, wokwi.com/projects/new/arduino-uno, which skips straight to that page.

The code editor already contains two empty functions:

That is the skeleton of every Arduino program, which Arduino calls a sketch. You will fill it in during the next lesson.

#A tour of the editor

The left side holds your files as tabs:

  • sketch.ino is your program, written in Arduino's version of C++.
  • diagram.json is a text description of every part and every wire in the circuit. When you drag parts around, Wokwi rewrites this file for you. You can also paste a whole circuit into it, which this course does often.
  • Library Manager adds code libraries for fancier parts such as displays. You won't need it for a while.

The right side is the simulation:

  • The blue + button opens the parts list (or press A while the diagram is selected). Pick a part and it appears on the canvas, ready to drag into place.
  • To draw a wire, click one pin, then click another.
  • The green play button compiles your sketch and starts the simulated board. While it runs, the same spot shows a stop button.
  • The Serial Monitor, a text panel for messages from your program, appears under the diagram as soon as your sketch prints something.

Across the top are Save and Share. Saving needs a free account, which lesson 3 of this module covers.

#A tour of the Arduino Uno

The Uno is a small board built around one chip, the ATmega328P microcontroller. Your sketch runs on that chip, and the chip talks to the outside world through the metal pins along the board's edges. Zoom in on the Wokwi drawing (press + or scroll) and find each group:

Pins Label on the board What they do
Digital pins 0 to 13 Read or write on/off signals. Pins 0 and 1 also carry the USB serial link, so leave them free.
PWM pins 3, 5, 6, 9, 10, 11 (marked with ~) Can fake an "in-between" output by switching very fast, for dimming LEDs and setting motor speed
Analog inputs A0 to A5 Measure a voltage between 0 and 5 volts and turn it into a number
Power 5V, 3.3V, GND Supply power to your circuit. GND (ground) is the 0-volt reference, and there are three GND pins.
Built-in LED the tiny LED marked L Wired inside the board to pin 13, so you can blink it with no extra parts

📝 Note

In Wokwi, the Uno's 3.3V, IOREF, AREF, and RESET pins are not simulated. Everything in this course uses 5V and GND instead.

#Prove it works with the official Blink example

Wokwi's documentation links to a ready-made Blink project. Open wokwi.com/projects/344891652101374548, then click the green play button.

If the L LED blinks, your browser can run every lesson in this course. Close that tab without saving; you will write your own version next.

#Set up for your computer

Wokwi behaves the same everywhere, so the differences are keyboard shortcuts and, if you have a real board, how you load code onto it.

Windows

  • Use Chrome, Edge, or Firefox. Undo in the diagram is Ctrl+Z, copy is Ctrl+C, paste is Ctrl+V.
  • Real board (optional): download Arduino IDE 2 from arduino.cc/en/software and run the installer. Plug the Uno in with a USB cable, then pick the board and its COM port from the board menu at the top of the IDE.

macOS

  • Use Safari, Chrome, or Firefox. The shortcuts use ⌘ instead of Ctrl: ⌘Z undoes, ⌘C copies, ⌘V pastes.
  • Real board (optional): download Arduino IDE 2 from arduino.cc/en/software, open the downloaded file, and drag the app into Applications. The Uno's port name starts with /dev/cu.usbmodem or /dev/cu.usbserial.

Chromebook

  • Use Chrome. Wokwi needs no Linux setup or app.
  • Real board (optional): ChromeOS can't run the desktop Arduino IDE. Use the free Arduino Cloud Editor at app.arduino.cc instead (it needs a free Arduino account), which uploads to an Uno through Chrome.

#Tinkercad Circuits, the backup simulator

If Wokwi is blocked on your network, Tinkercad Circuits (tinkercad.com/circuits) from Autodesk also simulates an Arduino Uno with breadboards, LEDs, and sensors. It needs a free account; students usually join through a teacher's class link, or set one up with a parent. The lessons in this course are written for Wokwi, but the code is the same Arduino code, so it runs in Tinkercad's text code mode too.

#Fixes for the problems beginners actually hit

  • The Wokwi page is blank or never loads. School and library networks sometimes block simulator sites. Try a different network, or use Tinkercad Circuits. Also try another browser, and close extra tabs on an older laptop.
  • I pressed play and it spins for a while. The first run compiles your sketch, which takes a few seconds and needs the internet. If it never starts, reload the page; your code stays in the editor until you close the tab.
  • Keyboard shortcuts like A or R do nothing. Click an empty spot on the diagram first, so it has focus. In Firefox, the setting Search for text when you start typing steals those keys; turn it off in Firefox's settings.
  • I closed the tab and my work is gone. Without an account, Wokwi doesn't keep your project. Lesson 3 of this module shows two ways to save, one of which needs no account.
  • (Real board) The IDE shows no port. Some USB cables only carry power, with no data wires. Try a different cable. Many low-cost compatible boards use a CH340 USB chip, and on older systems that chip needs a driver from the board seller's instructions.

Check your understanding

3 questions

1You want to dim an LED smoothly. Which pin should it connect to?

  • Pin 7 is a plain digital pin: it can only be fully on or fully off.

  • Pin 9 has the ~ mark, so it supports PWM, which switches fast enough to look dimmed.

  • A0 is an analog input. It measures voltages; it doesn't output in-between levels.

Show answer

B. Pin 9 has the ~ mark, so it supports PWM, which switches fast enough to look dimmed.

2Your friend's project lives only in a Wokwi tab, and they never signed in. What happens if they close the tab?

  • Without an account, Wokwi doesn't keep the project for you.

  • Saving to Wokwi needs an account. Without one, copying sketch.ino and diagram.json into files is the backup.

  • The simulated board's memory disappears when the simulation stops.

Show answer

B. Saving to Wokwi needs an account. Without one, copying sketch.ino and diagram.json into files is the backup.

3Which file would you edit to change the color of an LED part without touching the code?

  • The sketch controls behavior, such as when the LED turns on, not what the part looks like.

  • It lists each part with its attributes, such as an LED's color, and every wire.

  • That tab adds code libraries; it doesn't describe the circuit.

Show answer

B. It lists each part with its attributes, such as an LED's color, and every wire.

Key takeaways

  • Wokwi runs an Arduino Uno in your browser for free; an account is only needed to save projects online.
  • sketch.ino holds your code, diagram.json holds your circuit, and the green play button runs both.
  • PWM pins are marked with ~, analog inputs are A0 to A5, and the L LED is wired to pin 13.
  • Real hardware is optional. If you add it later, Arduino IDE 2 (Windows, macOS) or the Arduino Cloud Editor (Chromebook) loads the same code onto a real Uno.

#Further reading

  • Wokwi diagram editor guide (opens in a new tab): every mouse action and keyboard shortcut for placing parts and wires.
  • Wokwi's Arduino Uno reference (opens in a new tab): which pins and features the simulated Uno supports.
  • Arduino UNO R3 documentation (opens in a new tab): the official specs and pinout for the real board.

m1-l2.html:
What you'll learn

  • Explain what setup() and loop() do and when each one runs.
  • Blink the built-in LED with pinMode, digitalWrite, and delay.
  • Send text from the board with Serial.begin, Serial.print, and Serial.println.
  • Read and fix the most common compile errors.

Making one tiny LED blink sounds like a boring first program. It is actually a full system test. When the LED blinks, you know your code compiled, the chip is running it, a pin is switching between 0 and 5 volts on schedule, and the timing is right. Every project in this course, robot included, sits on top of those four facts.

Open a fresh project at wokwi.com/projects/new/arduino-uno and keep it open for this whole lesson.

#The two functions every sketch has

An Arduino program has no main() that you write yourself. Instead, the board calls two functions for you:

  • setup() runs once, right after the board powers on or resets. Put one-time preparation here, such as telling a pin to act as an output.
  • loop() runs again and again, forever. When it reaches its closing brace, it starts over at the top.

If you have written a while True: loop in Python, loop() is the body of that loop, and setup() is the code just above it.

#Step 1: Blink the built-in LED

Replace everything in sketch.ino with this:

Press the green play button.

Line by line:

  • LED_BUILTIN is a name Arduino defines for the pin wired to the L LED. On the Uno it is pin 13.
  • pinMode(LED_BUILTIN, OUTPUT) configures that pin to drive a voltage instead of measuring one. Pins start as inputs, so this line is required.
  • digitalWrite(pin, HIGH) puts 5 volts on the pin; LOW puts 0 volts.
  • delay(500) pauses the whole program for 500 milliseconds (half a second). During a delay, the board does nothing else.

One trip through loop() takes 500 + 500 = 1000 ms, so the LED blinks once per second.

🧪 Try it yourself

Change both delays to 100. Then try 50 for the on-time and 950 for the off-time. The second version gives a short "heartbeat" flash, still once per second, because the two delays still add up to 1000.

#Step 2: Make the board talk to you

An LED can only say "on" or "off". To see numbers and messages, use the serial port: a text link from the board back to your computer. In Wokwi the Serial Monitor panel appears as soon as your sketch prints.

Run it and watch the Serial Monitor:

A new line arrives every second, in step with the LED. Three details matter here:

  • Serial.begin(9600) must run before any printing. The number is the baud rate, the speed of the link in bits per second. Wokwi detects it automatically on the Uno, but the real Arduino IDE needs you to choose the same 9600 in its Serial Monitor.
  • Serial.print writes text and stays on the same line; Serial.println writes text and then ends the line. That's why "Blinks so far: " and the number share a line.
  • int blinks = 0; sits outside both functions. If you declared it inside loop(), it would be re-created as 0 on every pass, and the counter would print 1 forever.

#Step 3: Check the timing with millis()

millis() returns how many milliseconds have passed since the board started. It keeps counting during delays, which makes it a good stopwatch. Add one line at the end of loop():

The times climb by about 1000 each pass. Your exact numbers may differ by a few milliseconds, because the code between the delays (printing, adding) takes a little time too, and that time adds up. Module 4 uses millis() to replace delay() entirely, so a sketch can blink an LED and watch a sensor at the same time.

#Proof that your setup works

Check all three before moving on:

  1. The L LED blinks once per second.
  2. The Serial Monitor shows the counter going up by one each second.
  3. Changing a delay and pressing play again changes the blink speed.

If all three happen, your lab works. If not, the next section covers the usual reasons.

#When it doesn't compile

Arduino code is C++, which is stricter than Python. When the compiler refuses your sketch, the simulation doesn't start and the compiler's messages appear instead. Read the first error; the later ones are often side effects of it.

A missing semicolon. Every statement ends with ;. Leave one off after digitalWrite(LED_BUILTIN, HIGH) and the compiler reports:

The message names the line after the mistake, because that's where the compiler noticed. Look at the end of the line above.

Wrong capitalization. Arduino names are case-sensitive. Typing pinmode instead of pinMode gives:

"Not declared in this scope" means "I have never heard of this name". Check the spelling and capital letters, or check that you declared the variable.

A missing closing brace. Delete the final } of loop() and you get:

Click just after each { and match it with its }. Indenting the code inside each pair makes a missing brace easy to spot.

⚠️ Watch out

Nothing appears in the Serial Monitor, and there is no error. You probably forgot Serial.begin(9600); in setup(), so the serial port never started. On a real board, a second cause is a baud-rate mismatch: if the Serial Monitor is set to 115200 while the sketch says 9600, you see scrambled characters instead of text.

#Running it on a real Uno (optional)

If you have a board and installed Arduino IDE 2 in the last lesson:

  1. Plug the Uno into your computer with a USB data cable.
  2. Paste the sketch into a new IDE window.
  3. In the board menu at the top, choose Arduino Uno and its port.
  4. Click Upload (the right-arrow button). The output panel reports when uploading is done, and the L LED starts blinking.
  5. Open Tools > Serial Monitor, and set the baud rate menu to 9600.

The code is identical to the Wokwi version. That is the point of simulating first.

Check your understanding

3 questions

1A sketch has delay(200) after the HIGH and delay(800) after the LOW. What does the LED do?

  • That would need a 200 ms cycle. Here one cycle is 200 + 800 = 1000 ms.

  • It is on for 200 ms and off for 800 ms, so you see a short flash every second.

  • The delays don't need to match; each one just sets how long its state lasts.

Show answer

B. It is on for 200 ms and off for 800 ms, so you see a short flash every second.

2You move int blinks = 0; from the top of the file to the first line inside loop(). What does the Serial Monitor show?

  • The variable is now created fresh at the start of each pass, so the count can't build up.

  • Each pass sets blinks to 0, adds 1, and prints 1.

  • Declaring a variable inside a function is legal; it just changes how long it lives.

Show answer

B. Each pass sets blinks to 0, adds 1, and prints 1.

3The compiler says error: expected ';' before 'Serial'. Where is the mistake most likely to be?

  • That line is where the compiler noticed the problem, not usually where it is.

  • The compiler only realizes a ; is missing when it reaches the next statement.

  • A missing Serial.begin doesn't cause a compile error; it just means nothing prints.

Show answer

B. The compiler only realizes a ; is missing when it reaches the next statement.

Key takeaways

  • setup() runs once at power-on, and loop() repeats forever.
  • pinMode(pin, OUTPUT) comes before digitalWrite(pin, HIGH/LOW).
  • delay(ms) freezes the program; millis() tells you how long the board has been running.
  • Serial.begin(9600) in setup(), then Serial.print/Serial.println, is how the board tells you what it's doing.
  • Read the first compile error, and check the line above the one it names.

#Further reading

  • Arduino's Blink example (opens in a new tab): the official version of this sketch, with a wiring diagram for an external LED.
  • Serial reference (opens in a new tab): every Serial function, including print options for decimals and number bases.
  • Wokwi Serial Monitor guide (opens in a new tab): how Wokwi's monitor opens, and how to type input back to your sketch.

m1-l3.html:
What you'll learn

  • Follow the course safety rules, including the one with no exceptions.
  • Save a Wokwi project with an account, or back it up without one.
  • Keep personal information out of public projects.
  • Debug a broken circuit with a fixed routine instead of random changes.

Most electronics accidents in school labs don't involve anything dramatic. They involve a 9-volt battery rolling around in a bag with some coins, an LED connected with no resistor, or someone rewiring a board while it's still plugged in. The rules below prevent all of those, and they apply from the first real part you touch.

#The safety rules for this course

Rule 1, the one with no exceptions: never work with mains power. Mains is the electricity from wall outlets (120 or 230 volts, depending on your country). It can kill. Nothing in this course plugs into an outlet except a USB charger or your computer. Don't open chargers or power bricks, don't wire anything to an outlet or extension cord, and don't follow online projects that do.

The power sources this course uses are low voltage:

Source Voltage Used for
USB from your computer 5 V The Uno and small circuits
AA battery pack (4 × AA) about 6 V Motors and robots, later
9 V battery 9 V Optional board power

Rule 2: unplug before you rewire. Moving a wire on a powered board is the easiest way to touch 5V to GND by accident. Pull the USB cable, change the circuit, check it, then plug back in.

Rule 3: every LED gets a resistor, and nothing connects 5V straight to GND. A direct wire from 5V to GND is a short circuit. Module 2 shows the math behind why that's dangerous for the board and the USB port.

Rule 4: feel, smell, look. If a part is hot to touch, if you smell hot plastic, or if the board's power light goes out, unplug immediately and find out why before powering it again.

Rule 5: treat batteries with respect. Never connect a battery's two terminals together with a wire. Store 9 V batteries with their terminals covered (their terminals sit side by side, so a coin or key can short them). Lithium packs (LiPo, Li-ion) are only charged with their proper charger, and a swollen, dented, or punctured one goes to a battery recycling point, not back into a project.

Rule 6: motors get their own power. An Arduino pin can't drive a motor. The motor modules show how to use a motor driver and a separate battery pack.

⚠️ Watch out

The simulator can't warn you about most of these mistakes. Wokwi's own documentation says its analog simulation is very basic, so a circuit that would overheat on a real desk may look perfectly happy on screen. Use the rules on real parts even when the simulated version worked.

#Saving your work in Wokwi

You have two options.

With a free account. Click Save. Wokwi asks you to sign in or create an account the first time. After that, your project gets its own web address (it looks like wokwi.com/projects/ followed by a long number), and Save updates it. Ask a parent or guardian before you create any online account.

Without an account. Back up the two files that make up a project:

  1. Click the sketch.ino tab, select all the text (Ctrl+A, or ⌘A on a Mac), copy it, and paste it into a plain text file named, for example, m2-led-resistor.ino.txt.
  2. Do the same for the diagram.json tab, into m2-led-resistor.diagram.json.txt.
  3. To restore, open a new Uno project and paste each file back into its tab.

Because diagram.json describes every part and wire, those two files rebuild the whole circuit.

#Name projects so you can find them

Use the module number and what the project does, like m3-button-led or m4-greenhouse-monitor. When you change a working project into something new, save a copy first instead of editing over the version that worked. Then you always have something to go back to.

#Privacy: free projects are public

On Wokwi's free plan, saved projects are public: the pricing page says free projects are "visible to everyone". So keep personal details out of them:

  • No real full names, school names, addresses, or photos in project titles, code comments, or Serial messages.
  • Pick an account username that doesn't identify you.
  • Only share a project link with people you'd show the code to anyway, such as a teacher or a help forum.

#Working comfortably: keyboard and accessibility

The Wokwi diagram editor can be driven mostly from the keyboard once a part is selected:

Key What it does
A Add a part
R Rotate the selected part 90°
D Duplicate the selected part
Delete Remove the selected part or wire
+ / - Zoom in and out
F Fit the whole diagram in the window
? Open the documentation for the selected part

Your browser's zoom (Ctrl and +, or ⌘ and +) enlarges the code text. If you use a screen reader, the code editor and the Serial Monitor are text, while the circuit drawing is visual. The diagram.json tab describes the same circuit in words, so you can read or build circuits by editing that file directly.

If colors are hard for you to tell apart, you are not stuck with resistor color bands or wire colors. In Wokwi a resistor's value is written in diagram.json, and you can change a selected wire's color with a number key (for example 0 for black, 2 for red), which helps if you choose colors you can tell apart.

#A routine for getting unstuck

When something doesn't work, changing random things wastes time and can hide the real fault. Use the same order every time:

The most useful tool on that chart is a breadcrumb print: a Serial.println that tells you where the program is and what it sees.

If "bright branch" prints but the LED stays dark, the code is fine and the problem is the LED circuit. If "bright branch" never prints, look at the numbers being compared. Each print cuts the search area in half.

#When you ask for help

Give the helper what they need to answer in one reply:

  1. What you expected ("the LED should light when I press the button").
  2. What happened instead ("it stays on all the time").
  3. The project link, or the two files.
  4. What you already tried ("swapped the LED, checked it's on pin 9").

Writing those four lines often solves the problem on its own, because you have to look at the circuit carefully to write them.

Check your understanding

2 questions

1Your circuit worked in Wokwi with an LED and no resistor. What should you do when you build it for real?

  • Wokwi doesn't model heat or current limits well, so "worked in the simulator" doesn't mean safe.

  • The real LED and pin need a resistor to limit current, whatever the simulation showed.

  • More voltage makes the missing-resistor problem worse, not better.

Show answer

B. The real LED and pin need a resistor to limit current, whatever the simulation showed.

2Your LED never lights. Serial shows reading = 812 and then bright branch. Where should you look next?

  • The print proves the if was taken, so the condition worked.

  • The code reached digitalWrite(9, HIGH), so the fault is between the pin and ground.

  • The sensor gave a sensible number and the branch ran; the input side is fine.

Show answer

B. The code reached digitalWrite(9, HIGH), so the fault is between the pin and ground.

Key takeaways

  • Never work with mains power. Use USB and small battery packs only.
  • Unplug before rewiring, put a resistor on every LED, and never wire 5V straight to GND.
  • Save with a Wokwi account, or copy sketch.ino and diagram.json into files; free projects are public.
  • Debug in order: compile, prove the code runs with prints, check the values, then check the wiring, changing one thing at a time.

#Further reading

  • Arduino: digital pins (opens in a new tab): the official explanation of how much current a pin can handle and what a short does to it.
  • All About Batteries (Adafruit) (opens in a new tab): battery types, capacity, and safe handling, written for makers.
  • Wokwi diagram editor guide (opens in a new tab): the full list of editor shortcuts, including wire color keys.

m2-l1.html:
What you'll learn

  • Explain voltage, current, and resistance in plain words, with their units.
  • Use Ohm's law (V = I × R) to predict a current before you build anything.
  • Calculate the power a resistor turns into heat, and compare it to the resistor's rating.
  • Explain why a short circuit is dangerous and why an LED needs a series resistor.

A team wires a red LED straight from an Uno's 5V pin to GND. It flashes very bright, then fades, and the plastic smells warm. Their code was fine; in fact there was no code at all. The problem is arithmetic, and by the end of these notes you'll be able to do that arithmetic before you plug anything in.

#Voltage pushes, current flows, resistance resists

Here's the intuition. Picture water in pipes.

  • Voltage is like the pressure difference between two points in the pipe. It is the push. It is measured in volts (V), and it always describes two points: "5 volts" on an Arduino means 5 volts higher than GND.
  • Current is how much charge flows past a point each second, like liters of water per second. It is measured in amperes (A). Arduino circuits usually use milliamps (mA): 1 A = 1000 mA.
  • Resistance is how hard a part makes it for current to get through, like a narrow section of pipe. It is measured in ohms (Ω). 1 kΩ (kilohm) = 1000 Ω.

Current only flows around a complete loop: out of the supply, through the parts, and back to the supply. Break the loop anywhere (a loose wire, a switch that's open) and current stops everywhere in that loop at once.

The water picture breaks down eventually (electrons don't leak out of an open wire end), but it gets the main relationships right.

#Ohm's law makes it precise

For a resistor, the three quantities are tied together by Ohm's law:

V = I × R, or rearranged, I = V / R

Double the voltage and the current doubles. Double the resistance and the current halves. Let's check a typical Arduino number: 5 volts across a 220 Ω resistor.

About 23 mA. Now let's see the pattern for a few resistors at once. Each line is one resistor; the steeper the line, the more current per volt.

Notice that every line passes through zero: no voltage, no current. And at 5 V, the 1 kΩ resistor allows only 5 mA, less than a quarter of what 220 Ω allows.

#Power: where the heat comes from

Every resistor turns electrical energy into heat. The rate is power, measured in watts (W):

P = V × I

The small resistors in starter kits are usually rated for ¼ W (0.25 W). Push more power than that through one and it gets hot enough to discolor, smell, or burn out. Let's check a few resistors connected straight across 5 V:

The pattern is worth remembering: smaller resistance means more current and more heat. Halving the resistance at the same voltage doubles the power.

#Short circuits: when resistance goes to almost zero

A short circuit is a path from the supply back to itself with almost no resistance, like a wire from 5V straight to GND. Ohm's law says what happens as R shrinks. Step through this and watch the current:

At 0.1 Ω the formula says 50,000 mA, or 50 amps. A real wire and battery can't quite deliver that, because the battery has a little resistance of its own, but they can deliver several amps. That heats the wire, the battery, and anything else in the loop. A USB port or board may shut off or be damaged. With a battery there is no computer to cut the power, so the wire just keeps heating up.

📝 Note

Why can you touch the 5 V pins safely, but not a wall outlet? Dry skin has a high resistance, tens of thousands of ohms or more, so 5 V pushes only a tiny current through you. Mains voltage (120 or 230 V) is 24 to 46 times higher, and a few tens of milliamps through the chest can disrupt the heart. That is why this course never uses mains power.

#Why an LED needs a resistor

An LED is not a resistor, and it doesn't follow Ohm's law. Below a certain voltage, called its forward voltage (about 2 V for a red LED, about 3 V for blue or white), almost no current flows. Just above it, the current rises extremely fast. The chart uses an idealized model of a red LED to show the shape:

So if you connect an LED straight to 5 V, nothing limits the current except the LED's own tiny internal resistance and whatever the supply can deliver. That's the flash-then-fade in the opening story: far too much current, too much heat, a damaged LED, and a stressed pin.

A series resistor fixes it. The LED takes its forward voltage, and the resistor takes whatever is left over. Since the resistor follows Ohm's law, it sets the current:

I = (V_supply − V_forward) / R

The resistor also makes the current stable. Real LEDs vary a little from one to the next, so look what happens if the forward voltage is a bit off:

A 0.2 V spread in the LED changes the current by less than 1 mA. Without the resistor, in the model above, the same 0.2 V spread would change the current by a factor of about 20.

#Batteries: voltage and capacity

A battery has two numbers worth knowing:

  • Voltage: an AA cell is about 1.5 V, so four in series give about 6 V. A 9 V battery is 9 V. A lithium cell (LiPo or Li-ion) is about 3.7 V.
  • Capacity, in milliamp-hours (mAh): roughly how long it can supply a current. A 2000 mAh battery could supply about 200 mA for 10 hours, or 20 mA for 100 hours. Real batteries deliver less at high currents, so treat it as an estimate.

Lithium cells pack a lot of energy into a small space. Shorted or punctured, they can overheat and catch fire, which is why they're only charged with a proper charger and never used if swollen.

⚠️ Watch out

Three classic mistakes. Mixing up milliamps and amps: 20 mA is 0.02 A, not 20 A. Put 20 into I = V/R as if it were amps and your resistor comes out 1000 times too small. Thinking the resistor "uses up" current: in a single loop, the same current flows through every part. The resistor drops voltage, and that sets the current for the whole loop. Worrying about which side the resistor goes on: before or after the LED gives exactly the same current, because both are in the same loop.

Check your understanding

4 questions

1A 1 kΩ resistor is connected across a 9 V battery. How much current flows?

  • That forgets the "k": 1 kΩ is 1000 Ω, not 1 Ω.

  • I = V / R = 9 / 1000 = 0.009 A, which is 9 mA.

  • That's R / V upside down. Current is voltage divided by resistance.

Show answer

B. I = V / R = 9 / 1000 = 0.009 A, which is 9 mA.

2Someone puts a 10 Ω resistor across the Uno's 5 V and GND pins. What happens to the resistor?

  • 10 Ω is a real value, but across 5 V it carries 500 mA.

  • P = V × I = 5 × 0.5 = 2.5 W, ten times the rating of a ¼ W resistor.

  • Ohm's law gives 5 / 10 = 0.5 A, which is 500 mA.

Show answer

B. P = V × I = 5 × 0.5 = 2.5 W, ten times the rating of a ¼ W resistor.

3Why can't you control an LED's current just by choosing the right supply voltage?

  • LEDs work over a range; the problem is how sensitive their current is to voltage.

  • Past the forward voltage, current climbs so steeply that small differences in the LED or supply swing the current wildly. A resistor smooths that out.

  • LEDs don't follow Ohm's law, which is exactly why they need one.

Show answer

B. Past the forward voltage, current climbs so steeply that small differences in the LED or supply swing the current wildly. A resistor smooths that out.

4An LED circuit is 5V → LED → 220 Ω → GND. Your friend says it's broken because the resistor is "after" the LED. Are they right?

  • Current doesn't arrive at the LED first. The same current flows everywhere in the loop at the same moment.

  • Both parts are in one series loop, so the resistor limits the current wherever it sits.

Show answer

B. Both parts are in one series loop, so the resistor limits the current wherever it sits.

Key takeaways

  • Voltage is the push between two points (V), current is the flow (A or mA), resistance opposes the flow (Ω).
  • Ohm's law: I = V / R. More resistance at the same voltage means less current.
  • Power is P = V × I. Kit resistors are usually rated ¼ W; less resistance across the same voltage means more heat.
  • A short circuit is a near-zero resistance path, so the current becomes huge and things heat up fast.
  • An LED's current shoots up past its forward voltage, so it always needs a series resistor: I = (V_supply − V_forward) / R.
  • Never use mains power. Low-voltage USB and small batteries are the only power sources in this course.

  • Light-Emitting Diodes (SparkFun) (opens in a new tab): forward voltage, polarity, and how to read an LED's datasheet.

What you'll learn

  • Calculate an LED resistor and round it to a value you can actually buy.
  • Check a design against the Uno's pin current limit and the resistor's power rating.
  • Wire an external LED in Wokwi by pasting a circuit into diagram.json.
  • Dim an LED with analogWrite and explain what PWM does to the current.

Last lesson ended with a formula. This one turns it into a working circuit: two LEDs on the Uno, each with its own resistor, fading in opposite directions. Before any wire goes in, Python will tell us which resistor to use and prove the design is safe.

Here is the circuit for one LED. The second LED is a copy on another pin.

#Step 1: Work out the resistor value

A typical red LED has a forward voltage of about 2.0 V. We'll aim for 15 mA: bright, but comfortably below the 20 mA that most small LEDs and Uno pins are rated for. The formula gives an exact value, but resistors come in standard sizes, so the code picks the next standard value up. These cells share variables, so later steps can reuse the function.

The exact answer is 200 Ω, but 200 isn't a standard value, so we use 220 Ω. Rounding up always gives less current than the target, which is the safe direction. Rounding down to 180 Ω would give 16.7 mA, more than we planned.

#Step 2: Check the pin and the resistor

Two limits matter. Arduino's Uno documentation lists 20 mA as the DC current per I/O pin. Its guide to digital pins says the chip can source up to 40 mA, but warns that overloading a pin can kill it, so treat 20 mA as your ceiling. And the resistor must not turn more power into heat than its ¼ W rating.

The resistor runs at about a sixth of its rating, so it will barely get warm. Now let's see how the current changes across the whole range of common resistors, so you know which values are off-limits for a red LED on a 5 V pin:

Notice how gently the current falls at the high end. 1 kΩ still gives 3 mA, which is dim but visible. When in doubt, a bigger resistor is the safe guess.

#Step 3: Wire it in Wokwi

Open a new Uno project. You could add the LED and resistor from the + menu and draw wires, but pasting the circuit is faster and guarantees the same wiring as this lesson. Click the diagram.json tab, select everything, and replace it with:

Each line in connections is one wire: from a pin, to a pin, then a color. Read it as a sentence: pin 9 goes to one end of the resistor, the other end goes to the LED's A (anode, +) pin, and the LED's C (cathode, −) pin goes to ground. The resistor's "value": "220" sets its resistance in ohms. Drag the parts around if they overlap; the wires follow.

#Step 4: Turn it on

const int RED_LED = 9; gives the pin a name. When you move the LED to another pin later, you change one number instead of hunting through the code.

#Step 5: Fade it with PWM

Pin 9 has the ~ mark, so it supports PWM (pulse-width modulation). A PWM pin can't output 2.5 V. Instead it switches between 0 V and 5 V very fast (about 490 times a second on pin 9) and varies how much of each cycle is spent on. analogWrite(pin, value) takes a value from 0 (always off) to 255 (always on).

Your eye can't follow 490 flashes a second, so it sees the average as brightness. Importantly, while the pin is on, the current is still the full 13.6 mA our resistor allows. PWM changes how long the current flows, not how much, so the safety check from Step 2 still holds at every brightness.

💡 Tip

Move the LED to pin 8 (no ~) and run it again. The LED snaps between off and on instead of fading. On a non-PWM pin, analogWrite can only give fully off (values below 128) or fully on (128 and above).

#Step 6: Add a blue LED with its own resistor

Blue LEDs need more voltage, about 3.0 V, so they need a different resistor. Reuse the function from Step 1:

The blue LED gets 150 Ω. It goes on pin 10, which also has PWM. Each LED gets its own resistor: if two LEDs shared one resistor in parallel, the red one (lower forward voltage) would take nearly all the current and the blue one would barely glow.

#The finished circuit and program

Replace diagram.json with the two-LED version:

And the sketch, where the blue LED fades down while the red one fades up:

On a real breadboard the circuit is the same. The LED's longer leg is the anode (+) and goes toward the resistor and pin; the shorter leg, on the side with a flat edge on the LED's rim, goes to GND. The 220 Ω resistor has bands red-red-brown, and 150 Ω is brown-green-brown.

Check your understanding

3 questions

1The formula said 200 Ω. Why did we use 220 Ω instead of 180 Ω?

  • Both are 20 Ω away. The reason is which direction is safe.

  • 220 Ω gives 13.6 mA, under the target. 180 Ω would give 16.7 mA, over it.

  • Wokwi accepts any value in the value attribute.

Show answer

B. 220 Ω gives 13.6 mA, under the target. 180 Ω would give 16.7 mA, over it.

2Why are the LEDs on pins 9 and 10 instead of 7 and 8?

  • All the digital pins have the same current rating.

  • Only the pins marked ~ (3, 5, 6, 9, 10, 11) produce PWM on the Uno.

  • The serial link uses pins 0 and 1.

Show answer

B. Only the pins marked ~ (3, 5, 6, 9, 10, 11) produce PWM on the Uno.

3At analogWrite(9, 64), the LED looks about a quarter as bright. What is the current through it while the pin is on?

  • PWM doesn't reduce the current; it reduces the time the current flows.

  • During each "on" slice the pin is at 5 V, so the resistor sets the same current. Only the on-time changes.

  • analogWrite on a PWM pin has no threshold; 64 means on for about 25% of each cycle.

Show answer

B. During each "on" slice the pin is at 5 V, so the resistor sets the same current. Only the on-time changes.

Key takeaways

  • Resistor = (supply − forward voltage) / target current, rounded up to a standard value.
  • Check every design twice: pin current at or below 20 mA, resistor power below its ¼ W rating.
  • Every LED gets its own resistor, because LEDs with different forward voltages don't share current fairly.
  • PWM (analogWrite, 0 to 255, on ~ pins only) dims an LED by changing on-time, not current.
  • diagram.json describes a circuit as text, so you can paste, copy, and save circuits exactly.

#Ideas to extend it

  • Swap in an RGB LED (three LEDs in one package) with three resistors, one per color, and mix colors with three analogWrite values.
  • Make a "breathing" fade by stepping level with a sine curve instead of a straight count, so it lingers near dark.
  • The fade looks like it spends a long time near full brightness. Your eye's response isn't linear; search "LED gamma correction" to see how lighting designers fix it.

#Further reading

  • analogWrite() reference (opens in a new tab): PWM pins and frequencies for every Arduino board.
  • Arduino's Fade example (opens in a new tab): the official fading sketch, with a breadboard diagram for a real LED.
  • Wokwi LED reference (opens in a new tab): the LED part's pins and attributes, including how it shows PWM brightness.

What you'll learn

  • Predict currents with Ohm's law before building anything.
  • Choose and check LED resistors for different colors and supply voltages.
  • Combine resistors in series and parallel to make a value you don't have.
  • Recognize dangerous circuits, including shorts that only happen when a button is pressed.

Every exercise here can be solved on paper first. Do that, then run the solution to check yourself. The Python is a calculator you can trust, not a replacement for the reasoning.

Warm-up. Without code: what current flows when 5 V is across 1 kΩ? And 3.3 V across 330 Ω? (Answers: 5 mA and 10 mA. If you got 0.005 and 0.01, those are the same answers in amps.)

#Exercise 1: Predict three currents

A 5 V supply is connected across a 330 Ω resistor, then a 1 kΩ resistor, then a 10 kΩ resistor. Predict the three currents in milliamps, then write a loop that prints them.

Need a hint?

I = V / R gives amps. Multiply by 1000 for milliamps. Each time the resistance grows 10 times, what happens to the current?

Show solution

Ten times the resistance gives one tenth the current. That pattern lets you sanity-check any answer: a 10 kΩ resistor on 5 V can never carry more than half a milliamp.

#Exercise 2: Resistors for two new LEDs

Find a standard resistor (from the E12 list: 10, 12, 15, 18, 22, 27, 33, 39, 47, 56, 68, 82, times 1, 10, 100, …) for each design, rounding up, and report the real current:

  1. A white LED (forward voltage 3.1 V) on 5 V, aiming for 15 mA.
  2. A red LED (forward voltage 2.0 V) on a 3.3 V board, aiming for 10 mA.
Need a hint?

R = (supply − forward) / current, with the current in amps. For the white LED that's 1.9 / 0.015. Then find the smallest standard value at least that big.

Show solution

Both land on 150 Ω, for different reasons. The 3.3 V board has less voltage left over after the LED (1.3 V), so it needs less resistance for the same current.

#Exercise 3: Will this resistor overheat?

A student connects a 100 Ω, ¼ W resistor directly across a 9 V battery "to test it". Calculate the current and the power. Is the resistor safe? How long would a roughly 500 mAh battery last like this?

Need a hint?

Find I first, then P = V × I. Battery life in hours is roughly capacity (mAh) divided by current (mA).

Show solution

At 0.81 W the resistor carries more than three times its rating. It will get hot enough to burn a finger and may char. A 100 Ω load on 9 V would need a 1 W resistor, or a much larger resistance.

#Exercise 4: Make a value you don't have

Your kit has plenty of 220 Ω resistors and nothing else.

  1. What do two 220 Ω resistors give in series (end to end) and in parallel (side by side)?
  2. Which of those is safe for a red LED (forward voltage 2.0 V) on a 5 V pin? Use the 20 mA pin limit.
  3. A friend needs about 150 Ω for a blue LED (forward voltage 3.0 V) but only has 100 Ω and 47 Ω resistors. What should they do, and what current results?
Need a hint?

Series resistances add: R = R1 + R2. In parallel, current has two paths, so the total is smaller than either: R = (R1 × R2) / (R1 + R2).

Show solution

Series 440 Ω is safe but dim. Parallel 110 Ω pushes 27 mA, over the limit. For the blue LED, 100 Ω and 47 Ω in series make 147 Ω, close enough to 150 Ω, giving about 13.6 mA.

#Exercise 5: Spot the dangerous circuits

No code for this one. Which of these circuits are dangerous, and why?

  • A. 5V → 220 Ω → red LED → GND.
  • B. Pin 9 (set HIGH) → red LED → GND. No resistor.
  • C. 5V → pushbutton → GND.
  • D. 5V → 10 kΩ → pin 2, and also pin 2 → pushbutton → GND.
  • E. A loose 9 V battery in a pencil case full of paperclips.
Need a hint?

For each one, ask: when everything is connected (and any button is pressed), what is the total resistance in the loop? Then use I = V / R.

Show solution
  • A is safe. 3 V across 220 Ω is 13.6 mA.
  • B is dangerous. Nothing limits the LED's current except the pin itself. The LED and the pin can both be damaged.
  • C is dangerous, but only when pressed. Pressing the button connects 5V to GND through almost zero resistance: a short circuit. It looks harmless until someone presses it.
  • D is safe. This is a pull-up resistor. Pressing the button puts 5 V across the 10 kΩ resistor, so only 0.5 mA flows, and pin 2 reads LOW. Module 3 uses exactly this idea (with a resistor built into the chip).
  • E is dangerous. A 9 V battery's terminals sit side by side, so one paperclip can short them, and the paperclip heats up fast. Cover the terminals or keep the battery in its packaging.

#Exercise 6: How long will the batteries last?

A robot project will run from either a 9 V battery (roughly 500 mAh) or a pack of four AA cells (roughly 2000 mAh). Plot estimated run time against the project's current draw, from 20 mA to 200 mA, for both.

Need a hint?

Hours = capacity / current, with both in milliamp units. Make a list of currents, compute two lists of hours, and plot both against the currents.

Show solution

The AA pack lasts four times longer at every current, because it stores four times the charge. That is one reason robot kits use AA packs rather than 9 V batteries: motors draw hundreds of milliamps.

#Challenge: A tested LED circuit checker

Write check_led(supply, forward, resistor) that returns a tuple: the current in mA, the resistor's power in watts, and a verdict string. The verdict is "OK", "pin overload" if the current is over 20 mA, or "resistor too hot" if the power is over 0.25 W (check the resistor first, since it's the bigger hazard). Then test it with unittest, and print a table for red (2.0 V), green (2.2 V), and blue (3.0 V) LEDs with 150, 220, and 330 Ω on 5 V.

Need a hint?

Power in the resistor is current squared times resistance, or (supply − forward) × current. Write the tests first: what should check_led(5.0, 2.0, 220) return, and what about check_led(5.0, 2.0, 100)?

Show solution

Every combination in the table is OK, which matches what you found by hand: 150 Ω is the smallest safe choice for a red LED on 5 V, and anything larger only makes it dimmer. The 47 Ω on 9 V test proves the resistor check runs before the pin check.

What you'll learn

  • Say which breadboard holes are connected inside, including the power rails.
  • Describe a circuit as nodes, and spot a part whose legs share a node.
  • Read a resistor's color bands and find an LED's polarity.
  • Explain how a pushbutton, a pull-up resistor, and a potentiometer are wired.
  • Translate a schematic into a breadboard layout.

A student builds two LED circuits side by side. Every wire matches the diagram, both resistors are correct, and one LED stays dark. Swapping the LED doesn't help. The fault is invisible from above: both of that LED's legs are pushed into the same row of five holes. Under the plastic, that row is a single metal strip, so current runs along the strip and skips the LED entirely.

A breadboard only makes sense once you know where its hidden metal strips are.

#What's under the holes

A solderless breadboard is a plastic block with rows of holes, and under the holes are springy metal clips that grip a wire or a component leg. The clips are joined in a fixed pattern:

  • Terminal strips. Each numbered row is split into two groups of five holes: a–e on one side and f–j on the other. The five holes in a group are connected to each other.
  • The center gap. The channel down the middle separates the a–e group from the f–j group, so hole 10e is not connected to hole 10f.
  • Power rails. The long lines of holes along the edges, marked + (often red) and − (often blue), are connected along their whole length. On many full-size boards each rail is split in the middle; a break in the printed red or blue line marks the split.

Here is the same pattern as a map. Every ●─●─●─●─● group is one connected strip:

#Think in nodes, not holes

A node is a set of points that are all connected together, so they are all at the same voltage. On a breadboard, each five-hole group is one node, and each rail is one node (or two, if it's split).

A component does useful work only when its legs sit in two different nodes. A resistor with both legs in row 12, a–e side, is "shorted out": current goes along the metal strip and ignores it. That is exactly what happened to the dark LED in the opening story.

Here is a correct layout for an LED circuit, drawn as nodes. Each box is one node on the breadboard; each arrow is a part or a wire that bridges two nodes.

To check any breadboard, trace the loop node by node: from the pin, through each part, back to GND. If you ever pass through a part whose two legs are in the same node, or you reach a node with nothing leading out, you've found the fault.

#LEDs and resistors

LEDs have polarity. Current only flows from the anode (+) to the cathode (−). On a real LED the anode is the longer leg, and the rim of the plastic has a flat edge on the cathode side. Put one in backwards and it simply stays dark. With a resistor in the loop on a 5 V circuit that normally doesn't harm it, so flipping a dark LED is a reasonable first test. In Wokwi the LED's pins are named A and C.

Resistors have no polarity; either way round works. Their value is printed as colored bands. On the common four-band resistor, the first two bands are digits, the third is a multiplier (how many zeros to add), and the fourth (gold or silver, set slightly apart) is the tolerance.

Color Digit Color Digit
black 0 green 5
brown 1 blue 6
red 2 violet 7
orange 3 grey 8
yellow 4 white 9

So red-red-brown means 2, 2, then one zero: 220 Ω. Gold tolerance means the real value is within ±5%. Here is the rule as code:

Notice that brown-black-orange is 10,000 Ω (10 kΩ): the third band is orange, meaning three zeros, not the digit 3. Precision resistors use five bands (three digits, then multiplier and tolerance), so count the bands before decoding. When colors are hard to tell apart, measure with a multimeter instead of guessing.

#Pushbuttons and the pull-up resistor

A small tactile pushbutton has four legs, but only two connections. The legs come in pairs that are always joined inside; pressing the button joins one pair to the other. In Wokwi, legs 1.l and 1.r are one pair and 2.l and 2.r are the other. Set the button's xray attribute to "1" in diagram.json and Wokwi draws the internal wiring for you.

On a breadboard, place the button across the center gap, so each pair lands in its own row. If you rotate it 90°, the always-joined legs end up on opposite sides, and the button looks permanently pressed.

There is a second trap. A pin set to plain INPUT with only a button attached is floating when the button is open: it isn't connected to 5V or GND, so it picks up electrical noise and reads random HIGHs and LOWs. The fix is a pull-up resistor that gently holds the pin at 5 V until the button connects it to GND. The Uno has one built into every pin, about 20 kΩ, switched on with pinMode(pin, INPUT_PULLUP).

This flips the logic: pressed reads LOW. It also explains why the button isn't a short circuit. When pressed, the 20 kΩ resistor sits between 5 V and GND, so only 5 / 20,000 = 0.25 mA flows.

Buttons have one more quirk: when the metal contacts close, they bounce apart and together several times within about a millisecond before settling. Your code can see one press as several. Wokwi simulates this bounce by default, and the practice lesson at the end of this module shows how to handle it.

#Potentiometers and buzzers

A potentiometer ("pot") is a resistor with a sliding contact, the wiper, controlled by a knob. Connect its two outer legs to 5V and GND, and the middle leg outputs any voltage between 0 and 5 V depending on where the knob is turned. Read it with analogRead, which gives 0 at one end, 1023 at the other, and about 512 in the middle. In Wokwi the pot's pins are labeled VCC, SIG (the wiper), and GND.

A buzzer makes sound. An active buzzer beeps on its own when given power. A passive buzzer needs a changing signal, which tone(pin, frequency) produces, so it can play different notes. Both connect between a pin and GND.

#Reading a schematic

A schematic shows which things are connected, not where they sit. Lines are wires; wherever lines meet with a dot, they form one node. These are the symbols you'll see in this course:

Part Symbol
Resistor A zigzag line (US style) or a small rectangle (European style)
LED A triangle pointing in the direction of current, with a bar on the cathode side and two small arrows pointing away
Pushbutton A line with a gap, and a small bar above the gap that bridges it when pressed
Potentiometer A resistor symbol with an arrow pointing at its middle (the wiper)
Battery Pairs of long and short parallel lines; the long line is +
Ground Three horizontal lines getting shorter, like an upside-down triangle

Turning a schematic into a breadboard layout is a matching job. Give each node in the schematic its own breadboard row (or a rail, for 5V and GND), then place each part so its legs land in the two rows it connects. The node diagram earlier in this lesson is that translation, written out.

⚠️ Watch out

Three layout faults that look fine from above. Both legs of a part in one five-hole group: the part is bypassed. Move one leg to another row. A circuit that uses both halves of a split power rail: the far half has no power. Bridge the gap with a short jumper, or keep everything on one half. A pushbutton turned 90°: it reads as always pressed. Rotate it so it straddles the center gap.

Check your understanding

4 questions

1An LED's legs are in holes 12a and 12e, and a resistor connects row 12 to pin 9. What happens?

  • 12a and 12e are in the same five-hole group, so both LED legs are on one node.

  • With no voltage between its legs, no current flows through the LED.

  • It's not about brightness; the LED is completely bypassed.

Show answer

B. With no voltage between its legs, no current flows through the LED.

2Is hole 20e connected to hole 20f?

  • Same row number, but on opposite sides of the center gap.

  • a–e and f–j are separate groups, which is why a button or chip can straddle the gap.

Show answer

B. a–e and f–j are separate groups, which is why a button or chip can straddle the gap.

3A button is wired between pin 2 and GND, with pinMode(2, INPUT_PULLUP). What does digitalRead(2) return while the button is held down?

  • With a pull-up, pressing connects the pin to ground.

  • The pressed button pulls the pin to GND; when released, the internal resistor pulls it back to HIGH.

  • Random values happen with a floating INPUT. The pull-up prevents that.

Show answer

B. The pressed button pulls the pin to GND; when released, the internal resistor pulls it back to HIGH.

4A pot's outer legs go to 5V and GND, and its middle leg goes to A0. The knob is turned a quarter of the way from the GND end. About what does analogRead(A0) return?

  • That's the reading with the wiper all the way at the 5V end.

  • A quarter of the way gives about a quarter of 5 V, and a quarter of 1023 is about 256.

  • That's the reading at the GND end.

Show answer

B. A quarter of the way gives about a quarter of 5 V, and a quarter of 1023 is about 256.

Key takeaways

  • Each five-hole group (a–e or f–j in one row) is one node; the center gap separates the two sides; rails run lengthwise and may be split.
  • Every part must bridge two different nodes. Two legs in one group means the part is bypassed.
  • LED: long leg (anode) toward the supply, flat edge (cathode) toward GND. Resistors: read digit, digit, multiplier, tolerance.
  • A button straddles the center gap. With INPUT_PULLUP, it reads LOW when pressed and HIGH when released.
  • A schematic shows connections, not positions: give each node its own breadboard row.

#Further reading

  • How to Use a Breadboard (SparkFun) (opens in a new tab): photos of real boards, rail splits, and common layouts.
  • Resistors (SparkFun) (opens in a new tab): color codes, power ratings, and series and parallel combinations.
  • How to Read a Schematic (SparkFun) (opens in a new tab): the full set of common symbols, with labels and node examples.

What you'll learn

  • Plan a breadboard layout from a schematic, one node per row.
  • Read a pushbutton with INPUT_PULLUP and handle its inverted logic.
  • Read a potentiometer with analogRead and scale it with map.

Here's the finished behavior. While you hold the button, the LED glows; the knob sets how brightly. Let go, and it goes dark. Four times a second, the board reports what it sees:

It's a small project, but it has the shape of nearly every robot program you'll write later: read a digital input, read an analog input, decide, then drive an output.

#The schematic, as nodes

There are three separate circuits sharing the Uno's 5V and GND:

#Step 1: Lay out the parts

In Wokwi, paste this into the diagram.json tab of a new Uno project. Wokwi lets you wire parts straight to each other, so this version skips the breadboard; electrically it's identical.

Notice the button uses 1.l and 2.l, one leg from each contact. Using 1.l and 1.r would connect two legs that are always joined, and the button would read as pressed forever.

On a real half-size breadboard, give each node its own row:

Part or wire Where its ends go Node it creates
Jumper Uno 5V to the + rail; Uno GND to the − rail Power and ground rails

LED Long leg in 9e, short leg in 10e Bridges row 9 to row 10
Jumper 10a to the − rail LED cathode to ground

Jumpers 16a to Uno pin 2; 18a to the − rail Button between pin 2 and ground

#Step 2: Prove the LED works first

Build in small steps and test each one, so when something fails you know which step broke it.

If it doesn't, check the LED circuit now, before the button and pot make things harder to untangle.

#Step 3: Read the button

Run it, then click and hold the green button.

digitalRead returns 1 (HIGH) while the button is up and 0 (LOW) while it's held. That's the pull-up at work: the pin rests at 5 V, and pressing connects it to GND. Get used to writing == LOW for "pressed".

#Step 4: Light the LED only while the button is held

There is no delay in this loop, so loop() runs many thousands of times a second and the LED responds instantly.

#Step 5: Read the knob

While the simulation runs, click the potentiometer, then use the Left and Right arrow keys to turn it. Page Up and Page Down make bigger steps, and Home and End jump to the two ends.

The reading goes from 0 at one end to 1023 at the other. analogRead measures the wiper's voltage: 0 V gives 0, 5 V gives 1023. Module 4 explains exactly how.

📝 Note

Wokwi's potentiometer documentation says it gives the same readings even if VCC and GND aren't connected, because the simulator doesn't fully model analog circuits. Connect them anyway. On a real board, a pot without both outer legs connected gives a floating, meaningless reading.

#Step 6: Turn the knob reading into a brightness

analogRead gives 0 to 1023, but analogWrite wants 0 to 255. Arduino's map(value, fromLow, fromHigh, toLow, toHigh) rescales one range to another. It uses whole-number math and throws away remainders, so let's check what it gives compared with simply dividing by 4:

They never differ by more than 1, and both reach exactly 255 at the top. Use map anyway: it says what you mean, and it still works when the ranges aren't a neat factor of 4 apart.

#Step 7: Combine everything and report on a timer

If the reporting used delay(250), the button would only be checked four times a second and would feel sluggish. Instead, the loop checks the clock each pass with millis() and prints only when 250 ms have passed since the last print. Everything else runs at full speed.

Run it, hold the button, and turn the knob. The output matches the preview at the top of this lesson.

The timer pattern is worth memorizing: subtract the last time from now, and compare with an interval. Writing it as millis() - lastPrint >= 250 (rather than storing a future deadline) keeps working even when millis() wraps back to zero after about 50 days.

Check your understanding

3 questions

1Why does the code check digitalRead(BUTTON) == LOW to mean "pressed"?

  • LOW means 0 volts; whether that's "on" depends on the circuit.

  • With INPUT_PULLUP the button pulls the pin down to ground, so pressed reads LOW.

  • With a pull-down resistor wired to GND and the button to 5V, pressed would read HIGH.

Show answer

B. With INPUT_PULLUP the button pulls the pin down to ground, so pressed reads LOW.

2What would change if Step 7 printed with delay(250) at the end of loop() instead of the millis() check?

  • The prints would look the same, but the inputs would only be checked once per delay.

  • delay freezes the whole loop, so the button and knob are only read four times a second.

  • It would print at the same rate. The difference is in how quickly everything else responds.

Show answer

B. delay freezes the whole loop, so the button and knob are only read four times a second.

3You move the LED to pin 8 without changing anything else (except const int LED = 8;). What happens when you hold the button and turn the knob?

  • Pin 8 has no ~ mark, so it can't produce PWM.

  • On a non-PWM pin, analogWrite treats values below 128 as LOW and 128 or above as HIGH.

  • analogWrite compiles for any pin; it just can't dim a pin without PWM.

Show answer

B. On a non-PWM pin, analogWrite treats values below 128 as LOW and 128 or above as HIGH.

Key takeaways

  • Build and test one sub-circuit at a time: LED, then button, then knob.
  • INPUT_PULLUP needs no extra resistor; the button goes between the pin and GND, and pressed reads LOW.
  • analogRead gives 0 to 1023; map(value, 0, 1023, 0, 255) turns that into an analogWrite brightness.
  • Use if (millis() - last >= interval) for repeated tasks, so loop() never stalls.

#Ideas to extend it

  • Make each press toggle the LED on and off instead of needing to hold it. You'll need to detect the moment the button changes, and deal with bounce; the practice lesson walks through both.
  • Add a passive buzzer on pin 8 and play tone(8, frequency) while the button is held, with the knob mapped to a frequency from 200 to 2000 Hz.
  • Add a second button that remembers the current brightness, so letting go of the knob doesn't matter.

What you'll learn

  • Trace a breadboard layout node by node and find a bypassed part.
  • Convert between resistor values and color bands in both directions.
  • Diagnose buttons that read "always pressed" or flicker randomly.
  • Count button presses reliably by detecting changes and debouncing them.

The first three exercises are about layout and need no simulator. The last three run in Wokwi; start from the button-and-knob circuit from the build-along, since it already has a button on pin 2 and an LED on pin 9.

Warm-up. On a half-size breadboard, which of these pairs of holes are connected? (a) 7a and 7d, (b) 7e and 7f, (c) 7a and 8a, (d) two holes in the same + rail, one at each end of the board. (Answers: (a) yes, same five-hole group. (b) no, the center gap. (c) no, different rows. (d) yes on a half-size board; on a full-size board, only if the rail isn't split in the middle.)

#Exercise 1: Find the bypassed part

This layout should light an LED from pin 6, but the LED stays dark. Trace it node by node and find the fault.

Part Placement
Jumper Uno pin 6 to hole 3a
330 Ω resistor 3c to 7c
LED Long leg in 7d, short leg in 7e
Jumper 8a to the − rail
Jumper − rail to Uno GND
Need a hint?

Write down which node each leg of each part is in: "row 3 (a–e)", "row 7 (a–e)", and so on. Does every part connect two different nodes? Does the loop make it all the way from pin 6 to GND?

Show solution

Both LED legs are in row 7 (7d and 7e are in the same five-hole group), so the LED is bypassed. There's a second problem hiding behind it: nothing connects row 7 to row 8, so the loop is also open.

Moving the LED's short leg from 7e to 8e fixes both at once. The loop becomes: pin 6 → row 3 → resistor → row 7 → LED → row 8 → jumper → − rail → GND.

#Exercise 2: Color bands in both directions

Write encode(ohms) that returns the first three bands for a value (assume two significant digits and gold tolerance), and use the decoder from the notes to check it round-trips. Test with 220, 330, 4700, and 10000.

Need a hint?

Keep dividing by 10 until the value is a two-digit number (10 to 99), and count how many times you divided. That count is the multiplier band's digit.

Show solution

The multiplier band is just "how many zeros", which is why 10 kΩ ends in orange (3 zeros) and 220 Ω ends in brown (1 zero).

#Exercise 3: From schematic to breadboard

Write a row-by-row breadboard plan for this circuit: a green LED on pin 3 with a 330 Ω resistor, and a pushbutton between pin 4 and GND (to be read with INPUT_PULLUP).

Need a hint?

Count the nodes first. The LED circuit has three (pin 3's wire, the resistor-to-LED junction, the LED-to-ground junction) and the button circuit has two. Ground can share the − rail. Remember the button straddles the center gap.

Show solution

One plan that works (yours can use different row numbers, as long as each node has its own row):

Part or wire Placement
Jumper Uno GND to the − rail
Jumper Uno pin 3 to 2a
330 Ω resistor 2c to 6c
Green LED Long leg 6e, short leg 7e
Jumper 7a to the − rail
Pushbutton Straddles the gap, legs in rows 12 and 14
Jumpers 12a to Uno pin 4; 14a to the − rail

Check it the way you checked Exercise 1: every part bridges two different rows, and both loops end at the − rail.

#Exercise 4: Two broken buttons

Two students run Step 3 of the build-along (print digitalRead(2) every 200 ms).

  • Student A sees 0 every time, pressed or not. Their diagram.json has ["btn1:1.l", "uno:2", ...] and ["btn1:1.r", "uno:GND.2", ...].
  • Student B wired the button correctly but wrote pinMode(2, INPUT);. On their real breadboard, when the button is released the output jumps between 0 and 1 at random, and changes when they wave a hand near the wires.

Explain each fault and fix it.

Need a hint?

For A: which button pins are always joined, pressed or not? For B: what is pin 2 connected to while the button is open?

Show solution

Student A connected pin 2 and GND through 1.l and 1.r, two legs of the same contact, which are always joined. The pin is permanently grounded, so it always reads 0. Fix: use one leg from each contact.

Student B's pin is floating when the button is open: connected to nothing, so it drifts with electrical noise, including the noise from a nearby hand. Fix: turn on the internal pull-up.

#Exercise 5: Count presses, not loops

Print Presses: 1, Presses: 2, … exactly once each time the button goes down. A loop that does if (digitalRead(2) == LOW) presses++; doesn't work: it adds thousands per press, because loop() runs thousands of times while your finger is down.

Need a hint?

Count changes, not states. Remember the reading from the previous pass in a variable. A press is the moment the reading was HIGH last time and is LOW now.

Show solution

Click the button a few times in Wokwi. Sometimes one click prints two or three numbers. That isn't a bug in the edge detection. It's bounce: the simulated contacts open and close several times before settling, and each closing is a real falling edge. To prove it, add "bounce": "0" to the button's attrs in diagram.json; the extra counts disappear. Real buttons can't switch off their bounce, so Exercise 6 fixes it in code.

#Exercise 6: Debounce with a timer

The fix for bounce: only accept a new button state after the reading has stayed the same for a short time, such as 20 ms. Bounces are shorter than that; human presses are much longer.

First, model it in Python. The list below is a button sampled once per millisecond (1 = released, 0 = pressed), with bounces at each press and release. Count the falling edges in the raw signal, then write a debouncer and count again. Then write the Arduino version.

Need a hint?

Track three things: the last raw reading, the time it last changed, and the accepted ("stable") state. On each sample, if the raw reading differs from the last raw reading, record the time. If 20 or more samples have passed since that change and the raw reading differs from the stable state, accept it, and count a press if the new stable state is 0.

Show solution

The same logic in Arduino code, using millis() as the clock:

With bounce switched back on in Wokwi, each click now prints exactly one number. The cost is a 20 ms delay before a press counts, far too short for a person to notice.

#Challenge: A knob bar graph with a freeze button

Wire four LEDs, each with its own 220 Ω resistor, to pins 3, 5, 6, and 9. Light 0 to 4 of them like a bar graph as the knob on A0 turns. Each (debounced) press of the button on pin 2 toggles freeze mode, where the display holds still even if the knob moves. Print frozen or live when the mode changes.

Need a hint?

knob * 5 / 1024 turns 0–1023 into 0–4 with five equal bands. Light LED number i (0 to 3) when i < lit. For the toggle, reuse Exercise 6's debouncer, and flip a bool frozen where it used to count a press. Only recompute lit when not frozen.

Show solution

Each LED draws about 14 mA through its own resistor, so all four together stay well within what the Uno can supply. analogRead(KNOB) * 5 peaks at 5115, which fits in an int (the Uno's int holds up to 32,767).

m4-l1.html:
What you'll learn

  • Explain which voltages the Uno reads as HIGH, LOW, or neither.
  • Convert an analogRead value to volts, and back, without integer-math bugs.
  • Use the voltage divider formula to predict a light sensor's reading.
  • Convert thermistor and TMP36 readings to degrees Celsius.
  • Smooth a noisy reading with a moving average, and explain its cost.

A greenhouse controller prints light = 512. Is the greenhouse bright or dark? You can't say yet. That number went through three steps: light changed a sensor's resistance, a small circuit turned that resistance into a voltage, and the Uno turned the voltage into a number. To interpret a reading, you have to run those steps backwards. These notes go through each step.

#Digital inputs see only two answers

digitalRead asks a yes-or-no question: is this pin's voltage high or low? On a 5 V board like the Uno, Arduino's reference says a pin reads HIGH above 3.0 V and LOW below 1.5 V. Between those, the answer isn't guaranteed: the same pin might give either value.

Here's a voltage rising slowly from 0 to 5 V, and what digitalRead would make of it:

That's why digital sensors are built to snap cleanly between near 0 V and near 5 V: buttons, door switches, tilt switches, and the "DO" (digital output) pin on many sensor modules. It's also why a floating pin is a problem: it wanders around the middle band.

#analogRead turns a voltage into a number

The pins A0 to A5 connect to an analog-to-digital converter (ADC). The Uno's ADC has 10 bits, so it splits the range from 0 to 5 V into 1024 levels, numbered 0 to 1023. Each step is about 5 / 1024 ≈ 4.9 millivolts.

To go from a reading back to volts, Arduino's own examples multiply by 5.0 / 1023.0:

volts = reading × 5.0 / 1023.0

Some code, including Wokwi's sensor examples, divides by 1024 instead. The two answers differ by at most about 5 mV, less than one step, so either is fine for sensors.

The step size sets the finest change you can see. Zoom in on a tiny slice of the input range and the "smooth" analog reading turns out to be a staircase:

#Voltage dividers turn resistance into voltage

Many sensors don't produce a voltage at all. A photoresistor (also called an LDR, light-dependent resistor) just changes its resistance: high in the dark, low in bright light. A thermistor changes resistance with temperature. The ADC measures voltage, so we need a way to turn resistance into voltage.

The answer is a voltage divider: two resistances in series between 5 V and GND, with the output taken from the point between them.

The same current flows through both, so each takes a share of the 5 V in proportion to its resistance:

V_out = 5 V × R_bottom / (R_top + R_bottom)

When the photoresistor sits on the bottom, bright light lowers its resistance, so V_out and the reading fall. Wokwi's photoresistor module acts like this circuit with a 10 kΩ resistor on top: its documented readings and its lux conversion code both work out to that arrangement. Let's model the photoresistor (Wokwi's defaults: 50 kΩ at 10 lux, with a "gamma" of 0.7 describing how fast resistance falls with light) and check against the values in Wokwi's documentation: about 853 at 10 lux, 511 at 100 lux, and 170 at 1000 lux.

The model matches Wokwi's numbers to within one count. So in Wokwi, light = 512 means about 100 lux: a dim room, far darker than a sunny greenhouse. With a real kit you build the same divider from a bare photoresistor and a 10 kΩ resistor. Swap the two parts, and the reading rises with light instead.

#Reading temperature

Two temperature sensors are common in starter kits.

An NTC thermistor is a resistor whose resistance falls as it warms (NTC means "negative temperature coefficient"). In a divider with a 10 kΩ resistor, its reading converts to temperature with the Beta equation, the formula Wokwi's NTC sensor documentation uses (Beta is 3950 for that part, and 298.15 is 25 °C in kelvin).

The TMP36 is a chip that outputs a voltage directly: 0.5 V at 0 °C, rising 10 mV for every degree. So °C = (volts − 0.5) × 100.

Notice that the NTC reading falls as it gets warmer, while the TMP36 reading rises. You can't guess a sensor's direction; you read its documentation, or you test it.

Here's how common sensors produce their signals:

Sensor Signal How the Uno reads it
Button, tilt switch, door switch Digital: near 0 V or near 5 V digitalRead
Photoresistor, thermistor Resistance, turned into a voltage by a divider analogRead
Potentiometer, TMP36, soil moisture probe A voltage between 0 and 5 V analogRead
Ultrasonic distance sensor (HC-SR04) A digital pulse whose length depends on distance Timing the pulse, covered with robots later

Soil moisture probes deserve a warning: some give higher readings when wet and others when dry. Record a reading in dry soil and one in wet soil before writing any thresholds.

#Smoothing noisy readings

Real analog readings jitter. Electrical noise, a flickering light, or a loose wire can make a steady sensor read 510, 514, 507, 523, 511. A moving average keeps the last few readings and reports their average, so one odd value gets diluted. Step through this one with a window of 3, and watch what happens to the spike of 900:

The spike raises the average for three readings instead of appearing once at full size. Here's the effect on a longer, noisy signal where the light really does change halfway through:

That delay is the price of smoothing. A bigger window gives a calmer line but reacts more slowly. For a greenhouse, a few seconds of delay is fine; for a robot about to hit a wall, it might not be.

⚠️ Watch out

Classic analog mistakes. Integer math: float volts = reading * 5 / 1023; computes with whole numbers before storing, so a reading of 600 gives exactly 2.00 V instead of 2.93 V. Write 5.0 and 1023.0 to force decimal math. Reading a pin with nothing attached: an unconnected analog pin floats and returns drifting nonsense, often influenced by the pin next to it. If a reading wanders on its own, check the wire first. Mixing up A0 and 0: analogRead(A0) reads analog pin A0. Digital pin 0 is the serial receive pin.

Check your understanding

4 questions

1A sensor's digital output pin sits at 2.2 V. What does digitalRead return on a 5 V Uno?

  • HIGH is only guaranteed above 3.0 V.

  • LOW is only guaranteed below 1.5 V.

  • 2.2 V is in the band between 1.5 V and 3.0 V, where the result can be either.

Show answer

C. 2.2 V is in the band between 1.5 V and 3.0 V, where the result can be either.

2analogRead(A0) returns 614. About what voltage is on A0?

  • The Uno's analog pins only measure 0 to 5 V.

  • 614 × 5.0 / 1023 ≈ 3.0 V.

  • That would be a reading near 245.

Show answer

B. 614 × 5.0 / 1023 ≈ 3.0 V.

3A sketch has float volts = reading * 5 / 1023; and reading is 600. What does Serial.println(volts) show?

  • That's the right answer, but this line computes with whole numbers before storing the result.

  • 600 * 5 / 1023 is whole-number math: 3000 / 1023 = 2, then it's stored as 2.00.

  • Assigning an int to a float is allowed; it just loses the decimals that were already thrown away.

Show answer

B. 600 * 5 / 1023 is whole-number math: 3000 / 1023 = 2, then it's stored as 2.00.

4You change a moving average from 5 readings to 50. What happens?

  • You can't get both. A bigger window is smoother but slower.

  • Each new reading is only a fiftieth of the average, so a real change takes about 50 readings to show fully.

  • More readings dilute each random wiggle further, so the output does get calmer.

Show answer

B. Each new reading is only a fiftieth of the average, so a real change takes about 50 readings to show fully.

Key takeaways

  • On a 5 V Uno, digitalRead gives HIGH above 3.0 V and LOW below 1.5 V; anything between is not guaranteed.
  • analogRead turns 0 to 5 V into 0 to 1023, about 4.9 mV per step. Volts = reading × 5.0 / 1023.0.
  • A voltage divider turns a sensor's resistance into a voltage: V_out = 5 V × R_bottom / (R_top + R_bottom).
  • Sensors differ in direction: check whether yours reads higher or lower as light, heat, or moisture rises.
  • A moving average reduces jitter, at the cost of a delay that grows with the window size.

#Further reading

  • analogRead() reference (opens in a new tab): resolution and voltage range for every Arduino board.
  • Voltage Dividers (SparkFun) (opens in a new tab): the divider formula, worked examples, and sensor circuits.
  • Analog to Digital Conversion (SparkFun) (opens in a new tab): how ADCs work, with the math for converting readings.
