What you'll learn

  • Read two analog sensors and convert their values to volts and degrees Celsius.
  • Check a conversion formula in Python before trusting it on the board.
  • Smooth readings with a moving average stored in an array.
  • Sample, decide, and report on separate millis() timers.

A small greenhouse needs two decisions made all day: switch on a grow light when it gets too dark, and switch on a fan when it gets too warm. This build makes a monitor that does both, with LEDs standing in for the light and the fan. (Real motors need a driver circuit, which comes later in the course.) When it's finished, it prints a status line twice a second:

#Step 1: Wire the sensors and indicators

Start a new Uno project and paste this into diagram.json:

Both sensor modules take power from 5V and GND and send their analog output to their own pin: light to A0, temperature to A1. Each module already contains its voltage divider. With a real kit, you'd build the light divider yourself from a photoresistor and a 10 kΩ resistor, as in the notes, or use a TMP36 for temperature.

#Step 2: Print the raw readings

Never write conversions before you've seen the raw numbers.

Now, while the simulation runs, click the photoresistor and drag its light slider down toward darkness. Then click the temperature sensor and raise its temperature.

Both numbers move in the "wrong" direction: darker means a higher light reading, and hotter means a lower temperature reading. That's how their dividers are built (the notes showed why for light). This is exactly why you print raw values first. A threshold written with the wrong > or < would switch the grow light on in sunshine.

#Step 3: Convert to volts and degrees, and test the formula first

Volts is the formula from the notes. For temperature, the NTC module's documentation gives a Beta-equation conversion. Before trusting that formula in C++, check it in Python: generate the reading the sensor should give at known temperatures, convert it back, and compare.

Every temperature comes back to within a tenth of a degree, so the formula is safe to use. Each reading step is worth roughly a tenth of a degree near room temperature, so more decimal places than one would be pretending.

Now the same conversions in the sketch. log() in Arduino is the natural logarithm, matching Python's math.log.

Serial.print(value, 1) prints a float with one decimal place; without the 1 it prints two.

#Step 4: Choose thresholds from the physics

"Dark" should mean something real. If the grow light should switch on below about 50 lux, the photoresistor model from the notes says the reading at 50 lux is about 633. So "dark" is light > 633. For the fan, the code already has degrees, so the threshold is simply temp > 28.0.

#Step 5: Smooth both sensors

A moving average needs the last few readings. An array holds them, and an index walks around it, overwriting the oldest value each time. The array is a ring: after the last slot, the index wraps back to 0.

One detail matters at startup. If the arrays begin full of zeros, the first averages are far too low, and a light average near 0 looks like blazing sunshine, while a temperature reading near 0 doesn't convert to a real temperature at all. So setup() fills every slot with a real first reading.

#Step 6: Put it on two timers

Sampling every 20 ms keeps the average fresh. Printing every 500 ms keeps the Serial Monitor readable. Two millis() timers let both happen in one loop() without any delay.

#The finished program

Run it and move both sliders. The yellow grow light switches on once the light reading passes 633, and the blue fan light switches on above 28 °C. Because of the 10-sample average, each change takes about 200 ms (10 samples × 20 ms) to fully show.

Check your understanding

3 questions

1You lower the photoresistor's light level and the reading goes up. Why?

  • This is the expected behavior for this circuit.

  • A larger bottom resistance takes a larger share of the 5 V, so the output voltage and reading rise.

  • analogRead maps higher voltages to higher numbers; it's the voltage that rose.

Show answer

B. A larger bottom resistance takes a larger share of the 5 V, so the output voltage and reading rise.

2What goes wrong if setup() doesn't fill the sample arrays before the first average?

  • Global arrays start full of zeros, which aren't real readings.

  • A light average near 0 reads as very bright, and a temperature average near 0 doesn't convert to a real temperature.

  • Reading an array of zeros compiles fine; the problem is wrong values, not syntax.

Show answer

B. A light average near 0 reads as very bright, and a temperature average near 0 doesn't convert to a real temperature.

3Why does the sketch sample every 20 ms but only print every 500 ms?

  • It wouldn't damage anything. It would scroll too fast to read.

  • Separate timers let each job run at the speed that suits it, without delay blocking either.

  • An Uno can read an analog pin thousands of times a second.

Show answer

B. Separate timers let each job run at the speed that suits it, without delay blocking either.

Key takeaways

  • Print raw readings first, and find out which direction each sensor moves before writing thresholds.
  • Test conversion formulas in Python across known values before putting them in a sketch.
  • Choose thresholds from the sensor's model or calibration ("about 50 lux = 633"), not by guessing.
  • A ring-buffer moving average smooths readings; fill it with real data in setup().
  • Several millis() timers in one loop() let sampling, deciding, and reporting each run at their own rate.

#Ideas to extend it

  • Near 633, the grow light flickers on and off as the reading wobbles. Use two thresholds instead: switch on above 650, and off only below 610. This gap, called hysteresis, comes back when the course models states and feedback.
  • Add "serialMonitor": { "display": "plotter" } to diagram.json and print just the two numbers separated by a space, to watch them as graphs instead of text.
  • Convert the light reading to lux with the formula on Wokwi's photoresistor page, and print both.

#Further reading

  • Wokwi photoresistor sensor reference (opens in a new tab): the module's pins, its attributes, and the code that converts readings to lux.
  • Wokwi NTC temperature sensor reference (opens in a new tab): the source of this build's Celsius formula.
  • Arduino's Smoothing example (opens in a new tab): the official moving-average sketch, using a running total.

Thermistor divider Analog A0–A5 analogRead
Light module "DO" Digital Any digital pin digitalRead

Switches are just buttons that something other than a finger presses, so they get the same pull-up treatment. The A pins can also act as digital pins if you run out, but digital pins can't read analog values.

#Exercise 2: Readings to volts and back, without the integer bug

Write to_volts(reading) and to_reading(volts) for a 5 V Uno, and check that they round-trip. Then show what the buggy C expression reading * 5 / 1023 (whole-number math) gives for readings 100, 600, and 1000, next to the correct answer.

Need a hint?

to_reading is the formula turned around: reading = volts × 1023 / 5, rounded to a whole number. In Python, // imitates C's division of two ints for positive numbers.

Show solution

The round trip is only off by a few millivolts, less than one ADC step. The whole-number version throws away everything after the decimal point, so it can only ever answer 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, or 5 volts.

#Exercise 3: Read a TMP36

A TMP36 outputs 0.5 V at 0 °C and rises 10 mV per degree. Convert readings 143, 153, and 184 to °C. Then find the reading that means 30 °C, so a sketch could compare raw readings without converting each time.

Need a hint?

First convert the reading to volts. Then °C = (volts − 0.5) × 100. For the reverse, 30 °C is 0.5 + 0.30 = 0.80 V; turn that into a reading.

Show solution

In a sketch, the conversion is one line:

Each reading step is about 0.49 °C for a TMP36 on a 5 V Uno, so don't expect it to resolve tenths of a degree.

#Exercise 4: Pick the divider resistor

A photoresistor measures about 1 kΩ in bright light and 100 kΩ in darkness. It goes on the bottom of a divider. Which fixed top resistor, 1 kΩ, 10 kΩ, or 100 kΩ, gives the biggest difference between the bright and dark readings? Plot the reading against the photoresistor's resistance for all three.

Need a hint?

Reading = 1023 × R_ldr / (R_top + R_ldr). Compute it at 1 kΩ and at 100 kΩ for each choice, and subtract. Think about what happens when R_top is much bigger, or much smaller, than the photoresistor.

Show solution

10 kΩ wins with a spread of over 800 counts; the others manage about 500. A useful rule of thumb: pick a fixed resistor near the geometric middle of the sensor's range. For 1 kΩ to 100 kΩ, that's √(1,000 × 100,000) = 10 kΩ.

#Exercise 5: Two ways to smooth

A moving average of the last 8 readings is one way to smooth. Another is exponential smoothing, which needs only one variable: smoothed = smoothed + 0.2 * (raw - smoothed). Each new reading pulls the smoothed value 20% of the way toward it.

Apply both to a noisy signal that jumps from 300 to 700 at reading 40. For each method, find how many readings after the jump it takes to get within 20 of 700, and plot both.

Need a hint?

Use random.seed so the noise is the same every run. For the "within 20" check, loop over the smoothed list from index 40 and stop at the first value above 680.

Show solution

Exponential smoothing moves first (it jumps 20% of the way on the very first new reading), but the moving average finishes sooner: about 7 readings against 13 here. The moving average's delay is fixed by its window; the exponential one creeps up on the new value without ever quite arriving. Exponential smoothing's real advantage is memory: no array, just one float, which matters on a chip with 2 KB of RAM. On the Uno it looks like this:

A smaller factor (0.1) smooths more and reacts more slowly; a larger one (0.5) does the opposite.

#Exercise 6: Report light levels only when they change

With the Wokwi photoresistor module on A0, print dark, dim, or bright, but only when the category changes, checking every 250 ms with millis(). Use the model from the notes to set the boundaries: darker than 20 lux is a reading above 772, and brighter than 500 lux is a reading below 250.

Need a hint?

Write a function that turns a reading into a category number (0, 1, or 2). Keep the last category in a global variable, and print only when the new one is different. That's edge detection again, this time on a category instead of a button.

Show solution

At Wokwi's default 500 lux the reading sits right on 250, so the first line may be dim or bright. Starting lastCategory at -1 guarantees the first check always prints something.

#Challenge: Calibrate at startup

Hard-coded thresholds break when the sensor, the room, or the soil changes. Write a sketch that spends its first 5 seconds recording the lowest and highest readings on A0 while you sweep the sensor through its range (in Wokwi, use a potentiometer standing in for a soil probe, and turn it end to end). After that, print each reading as a percentage from 0 to 100 of the calibrated range, twice a second.

Need a hint?

Start low at 1023 and high at 0, so the first real reading replaces both. Inside a while (millis() < 5000) loop in setup(), update them. Afterwards, map(reading, low, high, 0, 100) gives the percentage, and constrain(…, 0, 100) stops readings outside the calibrated range from producing 110% or −5%.

Show solution

The high <= low guard matters: if nobody sweeps the sensor, low and high end up equal, and map would divide by zero. Real projects often save calibration values so they survive a restart, but recalibrating at power-on is a good start.

m5-l1.html:
What you'll learn

  • Explain why an Arduino pin cannot power a motor directly, using real current numbers.
  • Read an H-bridge truth table and predict whether a motor goes forward, backward, brakes, or coasts.
  • Wire motor power safely: separate supply, shared ground, and flyback protection.
  • Use analogWrite() duty cycles for speed and the Servo library for angle.

An Arduino Uno pin is happy supplying about 20 mA. The datasheet for its chip lists 40 mA as the absolute limit, the point where damage starts. Adafruit measured the small yellow "TT" gear motor that ships in most robot kits: 155 mA spinning freely at 4.5 V, and 1.2 A when the wheel is held still. A stalled motor wants sixty times what the pin is comfortable giving.

So the pin can't be the power source. It can still be the boss, telling a motor driver when to switch a big current from a battery.

#Servo or DC motor: pick the right actuator

Robots mostly use two kinds of motor, and they are controlled in completely different ways.

DC gear motor Hobby servo
What it does Spins continuously. More voltage, more speed. Turns to an angle (0 to 180°) and holds it.
How you control it A driver chip: two direction pins plus a PWM speed pin One signal wire that gets a pulse every 20 ms
Typical robot job Driving the wheels Pointing a sensor, steering, a gripper
In Wokwi No DC motor part, so LEDs stand in for the driver inputs Yes, wokwi-servo

Wokwi's parts list has a servo and stepper motors, but no plain DC motor and no L298N driver board. So the build in this module puts LEDs exactly where the driver's input wires would go. The code is the code a real robot runs; only the last few centimeters of wire change.

#Why a pin can't run a motor

Current is the first problem, and you've seen the numbers. There are two more.

Motors kick back. A motor is a coil, and a coil resists sudden changes in current. Switch it off and the voltage spikes far above the supply, straight into whatever just switched off.

Motors sag the supply. Starting a motor pulls a surge. If the Arduino shares that battery, its voltage dips and the board resets. A robot that "reboots every time it starts driving" is almost always this.

#The H-bridge: four switches that pick a direction

To reverse a DC motor you swap which terminal gets positive. An H-bridge does that with four electronic switches arranged like the letter H, with the motor as the crossbar.

Closing S1 and S2 together would short the supply to ground (shoot-through). Driver chips such as the L298N handle the switches for you, so you only set three pins per motor:

ENA (enable) IN1 IN2 What the motor does
HIGH or PWM HIGH LOW Forward
HIGH or PWM LOW HIGH Reverse
HIGH or PWM same as IN2 same as IN1 Brakes hard (both terminals tied together)
LOW anything anything Coasts to a stop (motor disconnected)

"Forward" just means one direction; if your wheel spins the wrong way, swap the two motor wires or swap HIGH and LOW in code.

#Give the motors their own battery, and share the ground

The safe layout has two power sources. The Arduino runs from USB (or its own regulator). The motors run from a battery pack wired to the driver's motor-supply terminal. The two systems share one thing: ground.

Why the shared ground? A signal of "5 V" means 5 V compared to something. Without a common ground the driver has no reference, and the motor twitches randomly or does nothing.

#Flyback: where the current goes when you switch off

Think of current in a motor coil as water in a long, heavy pipe. Slam a valve shut and the water hammers against it. A flyback diode is a bypass pipe: when the switch opens, the current loops back through the diode and dies away harmlessly.

In a one-transistor motor circuit you add the diode yourself, across the motor, stripe toward the positive supply. Most L298N modules sold for robots already include these diodes; check your board's description.

#PWM: speed from a switch that flips 490 times a second

An Arduino pin is either 0 V or 5 V, nothing between. Pulse width modulation fakes the in-between: switch fully on and off very fast, and vary the fraction of time spent on, the duty cycle.

analogWrite(pin, value) takes 0 (always off) to 255 (always on). On an Uno it works on pins 3, 5, 6, 9, 10, and 11, at about 490 Hz (980 Hz on pins 5 and 6). The motor's coil and weight smooth the pulses, so it responds to the average.

The pulses all reach 6 V. Only their width changes, and with it the average.

The chart hides a catch: a motor needs a minimum voltage to overcome friction. Here's a rough model of a TT motor on an L298N (which loses about 2 V inside the chip), with every assumption written down so you can change it:

Everything below 64 is a dead zone: the motor hums but the wheel doesn't move. Your motor's numbers will differ, but every DC motor has one.

Robot code usually describes speed as one signed number, −255 to 255, and a small function turns it into the three driver pins. Step through it:

Watch the last call: 400 is clamped to 255 first, so a bad calculation elsewhere can't ask the hardware for something impossible.

#Servos: a motor with its own feedback loop

A hobby servo hides a DC motor, a gearbox, a potentiometer on the output shaft, and a control chip. You send a pulse every 20 ms whose width (roughly 1,000 to 2,000 µs) names an angle. The chip compares it with the potentiometer and drives the motor until they match: feedback control, the big idea of the next module. The Servo library makes the pulses:

Each direction takes 181 × 15 ms, about 2.7 seconds, and during that time the Arduino does nothing else. Remember that; it becomes a real problem once a robot must watch a sensor while it moves.

⚠️ Watch out

Four classic motor mistakes.

  1. No shared ground. The driver ignores the signals or the motor jitters. Wire Arduino GND to driver GND.
  2. ENA jumper left on. On an L298N board the jumper ties ENA to 5 V, so the motor runs only at full speed. Pull it and wire ENA to a PWM pin.
  3. Servo plus PWM on pin 9 or 10. On an Uno the Servo library disables analogWrite() on pins 9 and 10, even with no servo there. Put motor speed pins on 3, 5, 6, or 11.
  4. Motors on the Arduino's 5 V pin. The surge resets the board.

Check your understanding

3 questions

1An L298N has ENA = 255, IN1 = HIGH, IN2 = HIGH. What does the motor do?

  • Forward needs IN1 and IN2 to be different. Here they match.

  • Both motor terminals are tied to the same side of the bridge, so the motor's own spinning is shorted out and it stops fast.

  • That would happen with a hand-built H-bridge closing S1 and S2, but the driver chip's logic prevents it.

  • Coasting is what ENA = LOW does: the motor is disconnected and friction slows it.

Show answer

B. Both motor terminals are tied to the same side of the bridge, so the motor's own spinning is shorted out and it stops fast.

2Your code calls analogWrite(5, 40) and the wheel doesn't move, but analogWrite(5, 150) works. What's the most likely explanation?

  • Pin 5 is a PWM pin on the Uno (at about 980 Hz). And 150 works on it.

  • About 16% duty gives an average too low to beat friction. The motor needs a minimum value before it turns.

  • The Arduino reference says you don't need pinMode() before analogWrite(). And 150 works without it.

Show answer

B. About 16% duty gives an average too low to beat friction. The motor needs a minimum value before it turns.

3A robot's Arduino resets every time both wheels start at once. Which change fixes the cause rather than the symptom?

  • The motors still pull the same surge; you've only slowed the program.

  • Lower speed may reduce the surge a little, but the Arduino still shares a sagging supply.

  • The surge now sags only the motor battery. The Arduino's supply stays steady.

Show answer

C. The surge now sags only the motor battery. The Arduino's supply stays steady.

Key takeaways

  • A pin supplies milliamps; a stalled motor wants over an amp. A driver switches battery current on the pin's command.
  • On an L298N, IN1/IN2 pick the direction and ENA sets the speed.
  • Motors get their own battery, everything shares one ground, and flyback diodes give switched-off current a safe path.
  • analogWrite(pin, 0–255) sets the duty cycle. Expect a dead zone at low values.
  • Servos take an angle with write(0–180). The library costs you PWM on pins 9 and 10.

#Further reading

  • Arduino Servo library reference (opens in a new tab): every function, plus the notes on pins 9 and 10 and on powering several servos.
  • analogWrite() reference (opens in a new tab): the PWM pins and frequencies for every Arduino board.
  • SparkFun: Pulse Width Modulation (opens in a new tab): duty cycle explained with clear waveform pictures.

What you'll learn

  • Turn one signed speed number into the IN1, IN2, and ENA signals an H-bridge driver needs.
  • Map a knob to forward, stop, and reverse, with a dead band around the middle.
  • Ramp speed changes so the motor never slams from full forward to full reverse.
  • Add a latching stop button and a servo needle that shows the speed.

Real robot teams don't test motor code on the robot first. They build a bench: a knob for the command, lights for the driver signals, and a big red button. That's what you'll make here, in Wokwi, and the sketch you end with is the motor layer of the robot you'll build later.

#What we're building

Turn the knob right of center and the IN1 LED lights while ENA glows brighter the further you turn. Left of center lights IN2 instead. The servo needle sits at 90° when stopped and swings toward 180° for full forward or 0° for full reverse. Press STOP and everything goes dark until you return the knob to the middle.

#Step 1: Set up the Wokwi project

  1. Go to wokwi.com (opens in a new tab), start a new Arduino Uno project.
  2. Click the diagram.json tab, select everything, and replace it with the diagram below. The parts appear already wired.
  3. Open the Library Manager tab, press the blue + button, search for Servo, and click it to add it.

Drag the parts around if wires overlap; positions don't affect the circuit. The knob's "value": "512" starts it centered (Wokwi's default is fully left, which would mean full reverse). The pins were chosen on purpose: ENA is on pin 5 because the Servo library switches off PWM on pins 9 and 10, and the servo itself is happy on pin 9.

#Step 2: One function that owns the driver pins

Everything the rest of the program says about the motor goes through setMotor(). Replace the sketch with this test, which runs a fixed pattern you can check by eye:

Press the green play button. You should see this repeating:

If ENA looks almost as bright at 80 as at 255, that's expected: Wokwi's LED model brightens short pulses the way your eye does with a real LED. The direction LEDs are the important check.

#Step 3: Read the knob, with a dead band

A potentiometer reads 0 to 1023. We want the middle to mean "stop", so subtract 512 to get a number centered on zero, then ignore small values. Without that dead band, a knob that's almost centered would creep the robot forward.

Put Serial.begin(115200); in setup() and print knobToSpeed(analogRead(KNOB)) in loop() to check it. Turning the knob fully one way should print about −255, the other way 255, and the middle 0.

#Step 4: Ramp instead of jumping

If you snap the knob from full forward to full reverse, the code above tells the motor to reverse instantly. On a real robot that's a current spike, a jerk that can flip the chassis, and stress on the gears. The fix is a ramp: each pass through loop(), move the actual speed at most MAX_STEP toward the target.

With a loop that runs every 20 ms, 0 to 255 takes about 51 steps, roughly one second. Here's the same logic run in Python so you can see the effect before you trust it:

The reversal takes about two seconds and crosses zero halfway, so the motor slows, stops, and then reverses. Change MAX_STEP to 15 and run it again: the robot gets snappier and the spikes get bigger. Picking that number is a trade-off you'll tune on a real chassis.

#Step 5: A servo needle that shows the speed

A gauge makes the invisible number visible. map() turns −255..255 into 0..180, so stopped is 90°.

#Step 6: A stop button that stays stopped

A stop button that only works while you hold it is a trap: let go and the robot leaps back to whatever the knob says. Ours latches. Pressing STOP sets a flag, and the flag clears only when the knob is back in the dead band, so the motor can never restart at speed by surprise. The button uses INPUT_PULLUP, so pressed reads LOW.

The flag starts true, so a robot switched on with the knob already turned stays still. Notice too that the stop skips the ramp. Ramps protect the hardware during normal driving; an emergency stop should act now.

#The finished sketch

Run it and turn the knob fully right. Lines like these scroll past as the speed climbs toward the target:

Now press STOP mid-ramp: speed drops to 0 on the very next line, and stays there while the knob is still turned.

#Taking it to a real robot

The sketch doesn't change. The wiring does:

Arduino L298N Notes
Pin 5 ENA Remove the ENA jumper first
Pin 7 IN1
Pin 8 IN2
GND GND Shared with the battery's negative
(nothing) Motor supply terminal (often labeled 12V) Battery pack positive (4 × AA works for TT motors)
(nothing) OUT1, OUT2 The motor's two wires

Before the first power-up, put the robot on a box with its wheels off the table. A bug that says "full speed" is harmless when the wheels spin in the air.

Check your understanding

3 questions

1Why does the stop button skip rampToward() and set the speed to 0 directly?

  • The ramp handles negative speeds fine; the chart shows it sliding to −255.

  • At MAX_STEP = 5, ramping down from 255 would take another second of driving after you hit STOP.

  • It can; 0 is a normal speed for setMotor().

Show answer

B. At MAX_STEP = 5, ramping down from 255 would take another second of driving after you hit STOP.

2Someone moves ENA to pin 10 to tidy the wiring. What breaks?

  • It does normally, but not while the Servo library is in use.

  • The direction LEDs still work, but analogWrite() on pin 10 no longer produces the right duty cycle.

  • The servo only needs its own signal pin, 9 here.

Show answer

B. The direction LEDs still work, but analogWrite() on pin 10 no longer produces the right duty cycle.

3What would happen without the stopped && target == 0 re-arm rule, if the flag simply cleared when you released the button?

  • The knob is still turned, so the target is still high. Latching until the knob is centered prevents the surprise restart.

  • That happens if the flag never clears at all.

  • The ramp slows the restart down but doesn't prevent it.

Show answer

A. The knob is still turned, so the target is still high. Latching until the knob is centered prevents the surprise restart.

Key takeaways

  • Keep all driver-pin logic in one function (setMotor) so the rest of the program speaks in signed speeds.
  • A dead band stops a nearly centered control from creeping.
  • A ramp limits how fast speed changes; it's gentler on gears, batteries, and chassis.
  • Emergency stops bypass the ramp and latch until the controls are back at zero.
  • Put the robot's wheels in the air for the first test of any new motor code.

#Ideas to extend it

  • Add a second motor (ENB on pin 6, IN3 and IN4 on pins 4 and 3) and a second knob, making a two-wheel "tank" control.
  • Make the ramp asymmetric: speed up gently, slow down faster.
  • Replace delay(20) with a millis() timer (the next module shows how) so the loop can do other work between ramp steps.

#Further reading

  • Wokwi servo part reference (opens in a new tab): its pins, range of motion, and example projects.
  • Wokwi Serial Monitor guide (opens in a new tab): including how to show the Serial Plotter instead of text.
  • Arduino: Basics of PWM (opens in a new tab): Arduino's own explanation of duty cycle, with waveform diagrams.

What you'll learn

  • Predict motor behavior from driver pin states.
  • Calculate current draw and battery runtime for a small robot.
  • Diagnose motor wiring faults from their symptoms.
  • Write motor and servo helpers that clamp, scale, and mix commands safely.

#Warm-up: duty cycle in your head

Before running this, guess the average voltage for analogWrite values 64, 128, and 191 on a 6 V motor supply.

A quarter, a half, three quarters: 255 is the full scale, so dividing by 255 gives the fraction of time the pin is on.

#Exercise 1: Read the driver like a truth table

An L298N channel has ENA, IN1, and IN2. For each row, say what the motor does: forward, reverse, brake, or coast.

ENA IN1 IN2
a 200 LOW HIGH
b 0 HIGH LOW
c 255 LOW LOW
d 90 HIGH LOW
Need a hint?

ENA decides whether the bridge is connected at all. If it is, compare IN1 and IN2: different means spin, the same means brake.

Show solution
Result Why
a Reverse, fairly fast IN1 LOW, IN2 HIGH is reverse; 200/255 is about 78% duty.
b Coast ENA = 0 disconnects the motor, whatever the IN pins say.
c Brake IN1 equals IN2 with the bridge enabled, so both terminals are tied together.
d Forward, slowly, or not at all 90 is about 35% duty; on a weak battery that may sit in the dead zone.

#Exercise 2: Skip the dead zone

Your motor doesn't turn below analogWrite 70. Write scaledPwm(percent) so that 0% gives 0 (stopped), and 1% to 100% spread evenly across 70 to 255. Sample output:

Need a hint?

Treat 0 as a special case. For everything else, the range 1..100 maps onto 70..255: start at 70 and add a fraction of the 185 counts left.

Show solution

Test the arithmetic in Python first:

Then the Arduino version. map() uses whole-number math, which is fine here:

map() rounds down rather than to the nearest value, so a few results differ from Python by 1. A wheel will never notice.

#Exercise 3: Will the battery last, and can it cope?

A two-wheel robot runs from 4 × AA NiMH cells rated 2000 mAh. Use Adafruit's measurements for TT motors at 4.5 V (155 mA running, 1.2 A stalled), and assume a micro servo draws 250 mA while moving and the Arduino plus sensor draw 60 mA. Find:

  1. The current while driving with the servo moving.
  2. The worst case: both wheels stalled against a wall, servo moving.
  3. Runtime at the driving current, if only 80% of the rated capacity is usable.
Need a hint?

Currents add. Runtime in hours is usable mAh divided by mA.

Show solution

The worst case is more than five times what a USB port supplies. That's the numerical case for a separate motor battery, and for code that stops the motors when the robot stops moving.

#Exercise 4: Find the wiring faults

Maya's robot resets every time the motors start, and the motor speed never changes no matter what analogWrite() she sends. Her wiring:

  • The L298N motor-supply terminal is wired to the Arduino's 5 V pin.
  • The L298N's GND goes to the battery's negative terminal only.
  • ENA goes to Arduino pin 10, and the ENA jumper is still on the board.
  • A servo on pin 9 uses the Servo library.
  • On her test bench, a third motor is switched by a single transistor with nothing across the motor.

Find at least four problems and the fix for each.

Need a hint?

Sort the symptoms: resets point to power, "speed never changes" points to the speed pin. Then look for anything missing that protects a transistor.

Show solution
  1. Motors powered from the Arduino's 5 V pin. The surge drags the Arduino's supply down and it resets. Wire a battery pack to the driver's motor-supply terminal.
  2. No shared ground. Add a wire from Arduino GND to the driver's GND.
  3. ENA jumper still on. It holds ENA at 5 V (full speed). Remove it.
  4. ENA on pin 10 with the Servo library. PWM is disabled on pins 9 and 10. Move ENA to pin 5 or 6.
  5. No flyback diode on the transistor circuit. Add a diode across the motor, stripe toward the positive supply, so switch-off spikes don't destroy the transistor.

#Exercise 5: A servo with safe limits

A servo aims an ultrasonic sensor, but the bracket hits the chassis below 30° and above 150°. Read a potentiometer on A0 and point the servo, never leaving 30..150. Print the angle when it changes.

Need a hint?

map() the reading to 30..150 directly, or map to 0..180 and then constrain(). Which one keeps the full knob travel useful?

Show solution

Mapping straight to 30..150 uses the whole knob for the safe range. The constrain() looks redundant, but it guards against a later edit to the map() line. Printing only on change keeps the Serial Monitor readable.

#Exercise 6: Two motors, one vocabulary

Add a second channel (ENB on pin 6, IN3 on pin 4, IN4 on pin 3). Write drive(left, right) that takes two signed speeds, then three helpers built on it: forward(speed), spinLeft(speed) (wheels in opposite directions), and stopAll().

Need a hint?

Write one function that takes the three pin numbers and a speed, then call it twice. Spinning left means the left wheel goes backward.

Show solution

setChannel packs the H-bridge logic into two lines: IN-a is HIGH only for positive speeds, IN-b only for negative ones, and both stay LOW at zero. With LEDs on all six pins in Wokwi, spinLeft lights IN2 and IN3 together.

#Challenge: Joystick arcade drive

Drive both motors from Wokwi's analog joystick: up/down is throttle, left/right is turning. Wokwi's docs say VERT goes from 0 (bottom) to 1023 (top), and HORZ goes from 0 (right) to 1023 (left). Its joystick only moves fully to each side, so test the corners and edges.

The standard mix is left = throttle + turn and right = throttle - turn. The catch: full throttle plus full turn gives 510, and constrain would chop it to 255 and change the turn. Scale both wheels down by the same factor instead.

Need a hint?

Find biggest = max(abs(left), abs(right)). If it's over 255, multiply both by 255.0 / biggest. Check the math in Python before writing C++.

Show solution

Full forward plus full right gives (255, 0): a pivot around the right wheel. Turn alone gives a spin in place. The Arduino version reads the joystick and reuses drive() from Exercise 6:

The long type matters: on an Uno an int tops out at 32,767, and 510 * 255 is 130,050.

m6-l1.html:
What you'll learn

  • Explain why a robot that decides from scratch on every reading twitches.
  • Replace delay() with millis() timers so the robot keeps sensing while it acts.
  • Design a state machine as a diagram and write it as an enum plus switch.
  • Use hysteresis and a proportional (P) controller, and predict what too much gain does.

Here's the first obstacle-avoider almost everyone writes:

In an empty hallway it looks great. Then it meets a wall at an angle, the reading hovers around 19 to 21 cm, and the robot buzzes in place: spin, drive, spin, drive, dozens of times a second, never committing to a turn. Nothing is broken. The code simply has no memory. Every 10 ms it makes a brand-new decision from one noisy number.

This lesson fixes that three ways: timers that don't freeze the robot, states that remember what it's doing, and feedback that reacts in proportion instead of all-or-nothing.

#The delay() trap

The obvious patch is "when you see a wall, turn for 600 ms":

The twitching stops, but now the robot is blind for 0.6 s. At 30 cm/s it travels 18 cm in that time without reading a single sensor, and a STOP button pressed during the turn is ignored. delay() stops everything.

The fix is to check the clock instead of waiting on it. millis() returns the milliseconds since the board started, as an unsigned long. Save the time something started, and each pass through loop() ask "has enough time passed?":

The line that matters is now - lastBlink >= BLINK_MS. Written as a subtraction of two unsigned long values, it keeps working even when millis() wraps back to zero after about 49.7 days. That's why every timer in this course looks exactly like it.

#State machines: give the robot a memory

A state is what the robot is doing right now: driving, backing up, turning. A transition is a rule for switching, triggered by a sensor reading or a timer. Drawing them first saves hours of debugging:

In Arduino code, an enum names the states, one variable holds the current one, and a switch runs only that state's code:

The robot reads the sensor on every pass, even mid-turn, yet it can't be talked out of a turn by one noisy number. Here's the same logic in Python, one sensor reading per step. Watch the 21 cm reading: the twitchy version would have driven forward again.

#Hysteresis: one threshold to enter, another to leave

Notice the two different numbers: turn when closer than 20 cm, but only drive again beyond 35 cm. That gap is hysteresis, and a thermostat uses the same trick so the heater doesn't click on and off every second. A noisy reading near one threshold can flip the decision; it can't jump a 15 cm gap.

Here's a robot creeping toward a wall with ±1.5 cm of sensor noise, decided both ways:

Each orange flip would be a real motor reversal: wasted battery and a robot that looks broken.

#Feedback: measure, compare, correct

So far the robot's choices are all-or-nothing. A line follower needs something finer. It has two light sensors straddling a dark line; when the robot drifts left, the left sensor sees more white than the right one.

The error is how far you are from where you want to be. A proportional controller steers by an amount proportional to it:

Small drift, gentle correction. Big drift, hard correction. Zero error, straight ahead. Sense, compare, act, repeat: that loop is feedback, and it's the same idea the servo used internally in the last module.

The one number you choose is the gain, KP. This simulation models a two-wheel robot that starts 2.5 cm off the line, with the sensor 12 cm ahead of the wheels, a 40 ms control loop, and motors that take 0.1 s to change speed:

Read the three curves. At 0.3 the robot corrects so gently that it swings wide and takes ages to settle; on a curve it would fall off. At 1.0 it overshoots, swings back a little, and settles within about a second and a half. At 6.0 it never settles: by the time the 40 ms loop and the slow motors have acted on a reading, the robot has already crossed the line, so it overcorrects the other way, forever. That wobble is the oscillation from the top of the lesson, now with a cause you can tune.

⚠️ Watch out

Three bugs that break state machines and timers.

  1. Calling enterState() every pass. Writing enterState(BACKING_UP) inside case BACKING_UP: resets the stopwatch each loop, so inState never reaches 400 and the robot backs up forever. Only call it when the state changes.
  2. Storing millis() in an int. On an Uno an int holds up to 32,767, so after about 33 seconds the timer goes negative and comparisons fail. Use unsigned long.
  3. Writing if (millis() > start + 500). It looks the same as the subtraction, but it fails when the clock wraps. Always write millis() - start >= 500.

Check your understanding

3 questions

1Inside case TURNING: someone adds enterState(TURNING); on the first line. What happens?

  • It isn't harmless here, because enterState also restarts the state's stopwatch.

  • stateStart is reset every pass, so inState >= 500 is never true and the exit rule can't fire.

  • Resetting the timer delays the exit; it never speeds it up.

Show answer

B. stateStart is reset every pass, so inState >= 500 is never true and the exit rule can't fire.

2A line follower with KP = 6 wobbles across the line nonstop. Which change is most likely to calm it?

  • The wobble comes from overcorrecting on stale information. Less gain, or fresher information, both reduce the overshoot.

  • More gain makes each overcorrection bigger.

  • A delay makes the information older still, which makes the wobble worse.

Show answer

A. The wobble comes from overcorrecting on stale information. Less gain, or fresher information, both reduce the overshoot.

3With "turn below 20 cm, drive again above 35 cm", the robot is TURNING and readings arrive: 22, 30, 34, 36. On which reading does it go back to DRIVING (ignoring the minimum turn time)?

  • 22 is above 20, but the exit rule needs more than 35.

  • Close, but 34 is not above 35.

  • It's the first reading past the exit threshold. The gap between 20 and 35 is the hysteresis.

Show answer

C. It's the first reading past the exit threshold. The gap between 20 and 35 is the hysteresis.

Key takeaways

  • Code that decides from scratch on every reading twitches near thresholds. States give the robot a memory.
  • delay() blinds the robot. Use unsigned long timestamps and millis() - start >= interval.
  • Draw the state diagram first; then code it as an enum, a switch, and an enterState() that resets the state's timer.
  • Hysteresis uses one threshold to enter a state and a different one to leave it.
  • A P controller corrects in proportion to the error. Too little gain is sluggish; too much, plus delay, oscillates.

#Further reading

  • Arduino: Blink Without Delay (opens in a new tab): the official example of millis() timing.
  • millis() reference (opens in a new tab): the return type, the wraparound, and why int causes bugs.
  • switch...case reference (opens in a new tab): the syntax, and what happens when you forget break.

m6-l2.html:
What you'll learn

  • Turn a written spec into a state diagram, then into an enum and switch.
  • Run three independent millis() timers in one loop(): sensor pings, door motion, and a warning light.
  • Move a servo smoothly with a proportional rule instead of jumping.
  • Test every transition by playing "the world" with Wokwi's distance slider.

Supermarket doors look simple until you list what they must never do: close on a person, stay shut while someone waits, or open and close so fast they look broken. That list is a state machine, and the door is an excellent rehearsal for a robot. Same sensor, same servo, same timers, but the stakes are easy to see.

#What we're building

Here is the spec, then the diagram it turns into:

  • When someone comes within 60 cm, the door opens to 90°.
  • It stays open while anyone is there, and for 3 seconds after they leave.
  • If someone appears while it's closing, it reopens. Always.
  • A red light flashes whenever the door moves.

Notice what isn't there: no arrow from OPENING straight to CLOSING. A person leaving halfway doesn't reverse an opening door; it finishes opening and waits. Missing arrows are design decisions too.

#Step 1: Set up the circuit

Start a new Arduino Uno project on wokwi.com (opens in a new tab), replace diagram.json with this, and add the Servo library through the Library Manager tab:

The sensor starts at 200 cm, so nobody is there. While the simulation runs, click the HC-SR04 to get a slider that sets the distance anywhere from 2 to 400 cm. That slider is you walking up to the door.

#Step 2: Ping the sensor on a timer

An HC-SR04 needs a 10 µs pulse on TRIG, then holds ECHO high for as long as the sound took to return. Sound covers about 0.0343 cm per microsecond and makes a round trip, hence the divide by 2.

Run it and drag the slider; the printed number should follow within a centimeter. Two choices here matter later. The 30000UL timeout caps how long pulseIn() can wait; without it, a missing echo stalls the whole program for its default of one second. And a timeout returns 999 ("nothing there"), not 0, because 0 cm would mean "someone is pressed against the sensor".

#Step 3: Move the door proportionally

door.write(90) would snap the door open in one jerk. Instead, every 40 ms we close a fixed fraction of the remaining gap between where the door is and where it should be:

That's the proportional rule from the notes: big error, big step; small error, small step. Here the "measurement" is our own doorAngle variable, not a sensor, so it can't oscillate the way the line follower did; the servo's built-in feedback loop handles the real shaft. Preview the motion before wiring it in:

KP = 0.5 slams open in a third of a second; 0.05 dawdles. We'll use 0.1.

#Step 4: The state machine

Now the diagram becomes code. Each case sets where the door should be and checks only its own outgoing arrows. enterState() logs every transition, which turns the Serial Monitor into a record of exactly what the controller decided and why:

The OPEN state has one subtle line. While someone is still there, it keeps pushing stateStart forward, so the 3-second countdown only begins once the doorway is empty:

#Step 5: The safety reversal and the warning light

In CLOSING, the person check comes first, before the "fully closed" check. If both were true on the same pass, safety wins:

The light is a third independent timer: toggle every 150 ms while the door moves, off otherwise.

#The finished sketch

#Step 6: Test every arrow

A state machine is tested by making each transition happen on purpose. Run these with the slider and check the log:

Test What you do What the log should show
Approach Slide from 200 to 30 cm CLOSED -> OPENING, then OPENING -> OPEN
Linger Stay at 30 cm for 10 s No new lines; the door stays open
Leave Slide to 200 cm About 3 s later, OPEN -> CLOSING, then CLOSING -> CLOSED
Safety Slide to 200, and while it's closing, back to 40 CLOSING -> OPENING
Brief visit Slide to 30, then to 200 before it's fully open OPENING finishes, then OPEN, then CLOSING after 3 s

A run through the first three tests prints something like this (your times will differ):

The slider said 30 and the log says 29, because converting to long drops the fraction. It doesn't matter for a door; module 7 shows when it does. If the safety test fails, look at the CLOSING case first.

Check your understanding

3 questions

1Why does the OPEN state set stateStart = now while someone is present, instead of just checking the timer?

  • stateStart only affects timing; the angle comes from doorTarget.

  • Pushing the start time forward keeps resetting the countdown while anyone is in the doorway.

  • millis() never stops; it counts from power-up regardless of state.

Show answer

B. Pushing the start time forward keeps resetting the countdown while anyone is in the doorway.

2Someone deletes if (someone) enterState(OPENING); from the CLOSING case. A person steps into the doorway while the door is closing. What happens?

  • Nothing tells it to stop; doorTarget is still 0 in CLOSING.

  • Without that arrow, CLOSING can only lead to CLOSED. The CLOSED state then sees the person and opens again, too late.

  • CLOSED does handle people, but the door has to finish closing before it reaches CLOSED.

Show answer

B. Without that arrow, CLOSING can only lead to CLOSED. The CLOSED state then sees the person and opens again, too late.

3readDistanceCm() returns 999 when pulseIn() times out. What would happen if it returned 0 instead?

  • The check is distanceCm < 60, and 0 is less than 60.

  • A timeout means no echo came back. Treating it as "very far" keeps the door shut.

  • The 30 ms timeout prevents long waits whatever value is returned.

Show answer

B. A timeout means no echo came back. Treating it as "very far" keeps the door shut.

Key takeaways

  • Write the spec as sentences, draw the state diagram, then code one case per state that checks only its own outgoing arrows.
  • Several millis() timers can share one loop() because none of them waits.
  • Give pulseIn() a timeout, and map "no echo" to a safe value.
  • A proportional step (error * KP) gives smooth motion that slows as it arrives.
  • Put safety checks first, and test every transition deliberately.

#Ideas to extend it

  • Add a "hold open" pushbutton: while held, the door stays OPEN no matter what the timer says.
  • Add a FAULT state: if the sensor returns 999 for 2 seconds straight, open the door and flash the light fast until it recovers.
  • Swap the servo for the motor test bench from the last module: the door becomes a robot that backs away when you approach.

#Further reading

  • Wokwi HC-SR04 reference (opens in a new tab): the pins, the slider, and the pulse-to-distance formula Wokwi uses.
  • pulseIn() reference (opens in a new tab): the timeout parameter and what the function returns when it expires.
  • Mermaid state diagram syntax (opens in a new tab): draw your own state diagrams in plain text, like the ones in this lesson.

m6-l3.html:
What you'll learn

  • Write several millis() timers and a servo sweep that never block.
  • Find and fix a fall-through bug in a switch-based state machine.
  • Design hysteresis thresholds and test them against a sequence of readings.
  • Tune a proportional gain and explain why a faster loop allows more gain.
  • Add a recovery state to a line follower.

#Warm-up: why the subtraction survives the wrap

An unsigned long counts up to 4,294,967,295 and then wraps to 0. Python's integers never wrap, so % 2**32 imitates the Arduino. A timer starts 100 ms before the wrap, and only 10 ms have passed. Predict which check fires early.

The addition wrapped to a tiny number, so the second check fired after 10 ms instead of 300. The subtraction measured the 10 ms correctly.

#Exercise 1: Three rhythms in one loop

Blink an LED on pin 12 every 250 ms, another on pin 13 every 1000 ms, and print alive with the time every 5 seconds. No delay() anywhere.

Need a hint?

One unsigned long "last time" variable per rhythm, and one if (now - last >= interval) block per rhythm.

Show solution

Adding the interval to last (rather than setting last = now) keeps each rhythm from drifting when a pass through loop() runs late.

#Exercise 2: Sweep a servo without freezing

The Sweep sketch from module 5 spends 5.4 seconds of every cycle inside delay(). Rewrite it so the servo on pin 9 still sweeps 0° to 180° and back at one degree per 15 ms, while a button on pin 2 (to GND, INPUT_PULLUP) lights the LED on pin 13 the instant it's pressed.

There's no Serial output to compare. Success looks like this: the servo sweeps without pausing, and the LED follows the button with no lag at any point in the sweep.

Need a hint?

Keep the angle and the direction (+1 or -1) in global variables. Every 15 ms, take one step and flip the direction at either end. The button check sits outside the timer block so it runs on every pass.

Show solution

The for loops are gone. Their job, remembering where the sweep is, moved into angle and stepDir, which survive between passes because they're global. That's the general recipe for turning any blocking sequence into a non-blocking one.

#Exercise 3: The robot that only reverses

This robot should drive forward until something is closer than 20 cm. Instead, with nothing in front of it, it backs up from the moment it's switched on, then spins, then backs up again. The log shows DRIVING -> TURNING and never mentions BACKING_UP. Find the bug.

Need a hint?

Read the DRIVING case line by line and ask where execution goes after its if.

Show solution

case DRIVING: has no break, so execution falls through into the BACKING_UP code. Every pass calls drive(160, 160) and then immediately drive(-120, -120); the last command wins, so the wheels turn backward. The fall-through code's timer check fires too: 400 ms after the robot entered DRIVING, it calls enterState(TURNING) straight from DRIVING, which is why the log skips BACKING_UP. Add break; at the end of the DRIVING case. The compiler won't warn you, so check by eye that every case ends in break.

#Exercise 4: Hysteresis for a cooling fan

A fan should switch on above 28 °C and off below 26 °C. Write fan_state(readings) in Python that returns the fan's state after each reading, starting OFF, and test it.

Need a hint?

Two rules, each checked only from the matching state: OFF looks for "above 28", ON looks for "below 26". Readings in between change nothing.

Show solution

The Arduino version is the same shape:

Readings like 27.1 and 27.5 fall inside the 2-degree band, so they leave the fan as it was. That band is what stops it clicking on and off.

#Exercise 5: A patrol route with a pause

Design a robot that drives a square: FORWARD for 2 s, then TURN for 0.7 s, four times, then DONE. At any time during FORWARD, an obstacle closer than 15 cm sends it to PAUSED; when the path is clear beyond 25 cm it resumes FORWARD with a fresh 2-second timer. Draw the diagram, then write the switch.

Need a hint?

Count completed sides in a variable that TURN increments when it finishes. DONE is reached from TURN when the count hits 4.

Show solution

The obstacle check comes before the timer check in FORWARD, so an obstacle at the 2-second mark pauses the robot rather than turning it into the obstacle. The 15/25 pair is hysteresis again.

#Exercise 6: Tune the gain, then speed up the loop

Using the line-follower model from the notes, find which gain settles inside ±0.3 cm fastest with a 40 ms loop. Then run the same gains with a 10 ms loop. What happens to Kp = 6, and why?

Need a hint?

"Settled" means the offset never leaves ±0.3 cm again. Find the last moment it was outside the band.

Show solution

With a 40 ms loop, Kp = 1.0 settles fastest; at 3 it takes over two seconds, and at 6 it never settles. With a 10 ms loop, Kp = 6 settles within about 0.6 s. The robot overcorrects when it acts on old information; a faster loop means fresher information, so it tolerates more gain. That's one more reason to keep delay() out of loop().

#Challenge: A line follower that finds its way back

On a sharp bend, both sensors can slide off the line onto white floor. A pure P controller sees zero error there and drives straight on. Add states: FOLLOWING (P control), SEARCHING (both sensors off the line for 200 ms: spin toward the side where the line was last seen), and STOPPED (searched for 3 s with no luck). In Wokwi, two photoresistor modules on A0 and A1 stand in for line sensors; with that module, less light gives a higher reading, so a dark line reads high.

Need a hint?

Remember the sign of the last error you computed while the line was visible, and use it to choose the spin direction. Inside a case, declaring a variable needs braces: case FOLLOWING: { ... break; }.

Show solution

The 200 ms grace period keeps a single dropout from triggering a search, and lastError is only updated while the line is visible, so a few frames of white floor can't erase the memory of which way it went. Your LINE_THRESHOLD will depend on your sensors; the next module shows how to measure it instead of guessing.

m7-l1.html:
What you'll learn

  • Write a test plan with measurable expected results, built from a baseline plus variations.
  • Log state and sensor data as CSV, and analyze a log to find flip-flopping.
  • Calibrate a distance sensor with a straight-line fit, and a line sensor with min/max readings.
  • Name common robot failure modes and the code that detects or survives each one.

Your obstacle-avoider dodged every box in your bedroom ten times in a row. At school, on the first run, it drove straight into a chair leg.

Nothing in the code changed. What changed was everything else: a thin round leg instead of a flat box, a smooth floor instead of carpet, a battery that had been on all morning. The HC-SR04 datasheet even says so: it wants a target of at least 0.5 square meters with a smooth, flat face. A chair leg is neither. Ten passes in one room didn't test the robot; they tested that room ten times.

#One success proves almost nothing

A test plan decides in advance what you'll vary and what counts as passing. Start by listing the factors that could change the robot's behavior, then the levels each one can take:

Twenty-four combinations is a lot of trials. Changing one factor at a time from a baseline gets you six, and when one fails you know exactly which factor did it. Add one "worst case" run (chair leg, carpet, tired battery) and you've covered most of what goes wrong.

Each test needs an expected result you can check with a number, not "it works":

ID Setup Action Expected Actual
T1 Box, 100 cm, tile, fresh Drive toward it Starts backing up between 15 and 25 cm
T2 Chair leg instead of box Drive toward it Same as T1
T3 Wall at 45 degrees Drive toward it Same as T1; no contact
T6 Battery after 20 min Turn after a stop Heading changes 70 to 110 degrees

#Make the robot tell you what it's thinking

You can't watch variables inside a moving robot, so make it describe itself. A log line every 100 ms, in comma-separated values, records time, state, the sensor, and the motor commands:

Why every 100 ms and not every pass? At 115200 baud each character takes about 87 µs to send, so a 25-character line costs around 2 ms. Once the Uno's 64-byte send buffer fills, Serial.print() waits, and your carefully non-blocking loop slows down. Remember from the last module what a slower loop does to a P controller.

Copy the log out of the Serial Monitor and the computer can read it for you. This sample came from a robot approaching a wall at an angle:

Six state changes in 600 ms, all at readings between 18 and 24 cm, is the signature of a single threshold with no hysteresis and no minimum turn time. The log turned "it acts weird near walls" into a cause you can fix.

#Calibrate instead of guessing

A calibration compares what the sensor says with what's actually true, then corrects the difference. For a distance sensor, put a target at measured distances, record readings, and fit a straight line. Here's what a session with a real HC-SR04 and a tape measure might produce (illustrative numbers):

A slope above 1 means every reading is stretched, which is what happens when the speed of sound in your room differs from the 343 m/s in the formula. Sound is about 6% slower at 0 °C than at 35 °C. Your code applies (reading - offset) / slope and the error shrinks to a few millimeters.

Line sensors need a different calibration because brightness depends on the room. Before each run, sweep each sensor over the floor and the line for a few seconds, keep the lowest and highest readings, and rescale to 0..1000:

Now "500" means "halfway between floor and line" under any lighting, so one threshold works in a dim gym and a sunny classroom. In Wokwi, drag the photoresistor's light slider up and down during those three seconds.

#Plan for how robots really fail

Every sensor and motor has known failure modes. Listing them before testing tells you which tests to write and what defensive code to add:

Failure What you see Cause Defense in code
No echo Robot hits a wall while the log says 999 Sound bounced off an angled or soft surface Treat several no-echo readings in a row as "unknown" and slow down
Spike One reading of 5 cm in open space Echo from something else, electrical noise Median filter: a single wild value never wins
Too close Readings jump around under 3 cm Below the sensor's 2 cm minimum Never let it get there: start backing up at 15 cm or more
Weak battery Turns come out short Time-based turns at lower speed Turn until the sensor sees clear space, not for a fixed time
Stuck Wheels spin, robot doesn't move Obstacle below the sensor's beam Watchdog: no distance change for 3 s while driving means STUCK
Lighting Line follower loses the line in sunlight Ambient light swamps the sensor Calibrate at the start of every run

Then iterate in a fixed rhythm:

The arrow back to "run the whole plan" matters. A fix for the chair leg can break the box test, and only rerunning every test (a regression test) catches it.

⚠️ Watch out

Testing habits that waste afternoons.

  1. Changing two things at once. If it improves, you don't know which change helped; if it gets worse, you don't know which one hurt.
  2. Only testing the happy path. The box in the middle of the floor always works. Test corners, angles, thin objects, and a tired battery.
  3. Trusting the simulator's sensor. Wokwi's HC-SR04 returns a clean, exact echo every time. Real sensors miss echoes and spike, so inject those faults yourself (the next lesson shows how).

Check your understanding

3 questions

1A robot turns 90 degrees with a fresh battery but only about 60 degrees after twenty minutes. The turn code is spinLeft(140) for 500 ms. What's the best fix?

  • That fixes it for a tired battery and over-turns with a fresh one.

  • A weaker battery means slower wheels, so a fixed time covers less angle. Ending on what the sensor sees works at any speed.

  • Logging helps you see the cause, but it doesn't change how far the robot turns.

Show answer

B. A weaker battery means slower wheels, so a fixed time covers less angle. Ending on what the sensor sees works at any speed.

2Which expected result belongs in a test plan?

  • Not measurable: avoids by how much, and how do you check it?

  • "Well" can't pass or fail.

  • Two things you can check from the log and by watching.

Show answer

C. Two things you can check from the log and by watching.

3Your fitted calibration line is measured = 1.04 x true + 0.5. The sensor reads 104.5 cm. What's the true distance?

  • Undo the fit: (104.5 − 0.5) / 1.04 = 100.

  • That applies the error a second time instead of removing it.

  • That removes the offset but not the 4% scale error.

Show answer

A. Undo the fit: (104.5 − 0.5) / 1.04 = 100.

Key takeaways

  • One success in one place proves little. Vary one factor at a time from a baseline, and add a worst case.
  • Expected results must be numbers you can check.
  • Log state and sensors as CSV every 100 ms or so, plus every state change. Logging every pass slows the loop.
  • Calibrate distance with a straight-line fit and line sensors with per-run min/max readings.
  • List failure modes before testing, and rerun the whole plan after every fix.

#Further reading

  • HC-SR04 datasheet (SparkFun) (opens in a new tab): range, beam angle, the 60 ms measurement cycle, and the target-size warning.
  • Serial.print() reference (opens in a new tab): formatting numbers, decimals, and bases in your logs.
  • Wokwi Logic Analyzer guide (opens in a new tab): record pin signals in a simulation when a log isn't detailed enough.

m7-l2.html:
What you'll learn

  • Build a logging harness that records raw and filtered readings with timestamps.
  • Use known slider distances to find and fix a systematic error.
  • Inject missed echoes, spikes, and phantom readings on purpose with a switch.
  • Implement a median-of-5 filter, test it against pass criteria, and measure the delay it adds.

Wokwi's HC-SR04 is a perfect sensor: set the slider to 100 cm and it answers 100 cm forever. Real ones miss echoes off angled walls, catch a stray echo from across the room, and occasionally report something 4 cm away that isn't there. Code tested only against a perfect sensor fails on its first real floor.

So this lesson builds a test harness: a small sketch whose whole job is to exercise one part of the robot, the distance reading, and print evidence. By the end, a slide switch injects realistic faults, and a filter you've tested handles them.

#What we're building

#Step 1: The circuit

New Uno project on wokwi.com (opens in a new tab); replace diagram.json with this:

The switch's middle pin goes to pin 4 and its right pin to ground. With INPUT_PULLUP, sliding the handle right pulls pin 4 LOW, which will mean "inject faults". It starts on the left: faults off.

#Step 2: Log first, and let the log find a bug

Before filtering anything, log the raw reading next to the time. Here's the reading function exactly as the door used it, plus a CSV line every 60 ms:

Now run a mini calibration: set the slider to 30, 100, and 250 cm and note what the log says at each. You'll likely see readings a little under the slider, such as 29 for 30. Wokwi's docs give its echo as about 58 µs per centimeter, so 30 cm makes a pulse near 1,740 µs, and 1,740 × 0.0343 / 2 = 29.84. Converting that to long throws away the .84, so the log says 29.

That's a systematic error: the same direction every time, so averaging won't remove it. Rounding does. This version stays in whole numbers (cheap on an Uno) and adds half a unit before dividing:

Rerun the three distances. The readings should now land within a centimeter of the slider. If 250 still shows 249, that's a different, smaller error: 58 µs per centimeter corresponds to sound at about 345 m/s, slightly faster than the 343 in our formula. That's a slope error, the kind the calibration fit in the notes removes.

#Step 3: Inject faults on purpose

Real sensors fail in three typical ways, so the harness fakes all three when the switch is on:

Add pinMode(FAULT_SWITCH, INPUT_PULLUP); to setup(). Slide the switch right and watch the raw column: mostly 100, with the occasional -1, 213, or 6. That's ugly, but it's honest, and a robot that brakes for every 6 will stutter across the room.

#Step 4: A median filter

Earlier in the course you smoothed readings with a moving average. An average dilutes a spike: one reading of 250 among four 100s averages to 130, which is still wrong. A median sorts the window and takes the middle value, so a single wild reading lands at one end of the list and is simply ignored.

Each sample goes into history[nextSlot], and nextSlot = (nextSlot + 1) % 5 wraps around, so the array always holds the latest five. Missed echoes are skipped instead of counted as 0, which would drag the median toward "obstacle!".

Before trusting it, test the idea in Python with the same fault rates, against a distance that jumps from 100 to 40 cm (someone stepping in front of the robot):

Two results. The median's worst error in the steady parts is zero, while the mean's is tens of centimeters. And the median takes a couple of samples to accept the new distance, because the old value is still the majority. At 60 ms per sample that's roughly 120 to 180 ms, or about 5 cm of travel at 30 cm/s. Filters always trade noise for delay; now you know the price.

#The finished harness

With faults on and the slider at 100, the log looks like this; the filtered column holds steady while the raw one misbehaves:

#Step 5: Run the harness tests

A harness earns its keep when the tests have pass criteria written down before you run them:

ID Setup Pass if
H1 Faults off; slider at 30, 100, 250 filtered is within 1 cm of the slider at each distance
H2 Faults on; slider at 100 for 30 s filtered never leaves 100
H3 Faults on; slider at 4 cm filtered stays near 4 even though phantoms read 3 to 9
H4 Faults off; jump the slider from 100 to 40 filtered reaches 40 within 3 samples
Write down what these tests can't catch, too. Every fault here comes from injectFault(), so H2 and H3 prove the filter handles the faults you imagined, at the rates you chose. Whether a real sensor facing a chair leg behaves like that is a question only real hardware (or a wider fault model) can answer. On a real Uno, randomSeed(analogRead(A5)) gives a different fault pattern each run; in Wokwi the unconnected pin may read the same every time, which conveniently makes a failing run repeatable.

Check your understanding

3 questions

1Why does medianCm() skip readings of -1 instead of sorting them in with the rest?

  • Insertion sort handles negatives fine.

  • -1 sorts to the bottom of the list, so two or three missed echoes would pull the middle value down toward an obstacle that isn't there.

  • The speed difference for five items is negligible; the reason is correctness.

Show answer

B. -1 sorts to the bottom of the list, so two or three missed echoes would pull the middle value down toward an obstacle that isn't there.

2Every log line reads exactly 1 cm less than the slider. Which fix addresses the cause?

  • A median removes random outliers, not an error that's the same every time.

  • The error comes from dropping the fraction when converting to long, which always rounds down.

  • More samples of the same biased number are still biased.

Show answer

B. The error comes from dropping the fraction when converting to long, which always rounds down.

3The median adds about 150 ms of delay. When would that matter most?

  • At higher speed the robot covers more ground during the delay, so it reacts later. Brake earlier, or drive slower near obstacles.

  • A stopped robot isn't covering distance during the delay.

  • At 50 cm/s, 150 ms is 7.5 cm, which can be the difference between stopping and touching.

Show answer

A. At higher speed the robot covers more ground during the delay, so it reacts later. Brake earlier, or drive slower near obstacles.

Key takeaways

  • Log first: a timestamped CSV of raw values exposes systematic errors like truncation.
  • A systematic error needs a correction (here, rounding); random errors need filtering.
  • Inject the faults the simulator doesn't produce: missed echoes, spikes, phantoms.
  • A median of 5 removes single outliers that an average only dilutes, and costs a few samples of delay.
  • Write pass criteria before running tests, and note what a test can't catch.

#Ideas to extend it

  • Count consecutive missed echoes and print WARNING: 3 no-echo readings when the streak hits 3.
  • Add a second column filter (mean of 5) to the log and compare them live in Wokwi's Serial Plotter.
  • Try a median of 3. Is the lag smaller? Does H2 still pass?

#Further reading

  • random() reference (opens in a new tab): the range rules (the upper bound is excluded) used by injectFault().
  • Wokwi slide switch reference (opens in a new tab): which pins connect in each handle position.
  • HC-SR04 datasheet (SparkFun) (opens in a new tab): the µs / 58 = cm rule of thumb behind Wokwi's sensor model.

m7-l3.html:
What you'll learn

  • Convert between echo time and distance, and correct for air temperature.
  • Write test plans with edge cases and measurable pass criteria.
  • Analyze logs and calibration data in Python.
  • Detect a stuck robot and replay recorded sensor data through a state machine to test it.

#Warm-up: echo time and distance

Sound travels about 0.0343 cm per microsecond, and the echo time covers the trip there and back. Predict the first number before you run this.

The last line explains the 30000UL timeout used throughout this course: an echo from anything within the sensor's 4 m range arrives within about 23,300 µs, so waiting 30,000 µs is enough, and waiting longer only freezes the robot.

#Exercise 1: The cold gym problem

Your code assumes sound travels at 343 m/s, its speed at about 20 °C. The speed changes with air temperature by roughly 331.3 + 0.606 × T m/s (T in °C). A target is exactly 100 cm away. What does the robot report at 5 °C and at 35 °C? Then write an Arduino function that takes the temperature into account.

Need a hint?

The sensor measures time. The real time is distance divided by the real speed; the code then multiplies that time by the speed it assumes.

Show solution

Cold air is slower, so echoes take longer and the robot thinks things are farther away: a robot that brakes at "20 cm" touches a little sooner in a cold gym. If you have a temperature sensor, use the real speed:

Dividing by 10,000 converts m/s to cm/µs (100 cm per meter, 1,000,000 µs per second).

#Exercise 2: A test plan for a line follower

Write at least six tests for a two-sensor line follower. Include at least two edge cases, and give every test a pass criterion you could check with a stopwatch, a ruler, or the log.

Need a hint?

Vary one thing per test: the track shape (straight, gentle curve, sharp corner, gap), the lighting, the starting position, and the battery. A sharp corner and a gap in the line are classic edge cases.

Show solution
ID Setup Pass if
L1 Straight line, start centered, room lights Completes 1 m without either sensor reading "off line" for over 200 ms
L2 Start 2 cm off center Back on the line (error under 10) within 0.5 s
L3 Gentle curve, 30 cm radius Completes it with no SEARCHING state in the log
L4 Sharp 90-degree corner (edge case) Enters SEARCHING at most once, and is FOLLOWING again within 1.5 s
L5 3 cm gap in the line (edge case) Crosses the gap and is FOLLOWING on the far side
L6 Bright sunlight on half the track Same as L1, after re-running calibration
L7 Battery after 20 minutes Same as L3
L8 Line removed entirely Reaches STOPPED within 3.5 s and stays there

L8 tests the failure path on purpose: a robot that keeps searching forever is a robot driving off a table.

#Exercise 3: Find the flip-flop bursts

Write find_bursts(rows, window_ms=500, min_changes=3) that returns the start time of every burst: a stretch where the state changed at least min_changes times within window_ms. Test it on this log.

Need a hint?

First build the list of times when the state changed. Then, for each change, count how many changes (including itself) fall within the next window_ms. Skip changes that belong to a burst you already reported.

Show solution

The BACKING_UP and TURNING changes at 2500 and 2800 are only 300 ms apart, but that's the robot doing its job, not flip-flopping: only two changes, below the threshold. Tuning min_changes and window_ms decides what "suspicious" means for your robot.

#Exercise 4: Two sensors that disagree

A robot sits perfectly centered over the line, yet the raw readings say left 500, right 570, so the P controller steers. Calibration sweeps measured left: white 180, black 820; right: white 240, black 900. Normalize both to 0..1000 and recompute the error.

Need a hint?

Normalized = (raw − white) / (black − white) × 1000. Do it for each sensor with its own white and black.

Show solution

The raw error of 70 was a difference between the two sensors, not between the sensors and the line. After normalizing, both read halfway between white and black and the error is zero. On the Arduino it's one line per sensor: map(constrain(raw, white, black), white, black, 0, 1000).

#Exercise 5: The one-second freeze

This robot runs smoothly until its ECHO wire works loose on a bumpy floor. Then it lurches: frozen for about a second, a sudden stop, frozen again. A loose wire is a hardware fault, but the code turns it into something much worse. Find both problems in the reading function.

Need a hint?

With the wire loose, ECHO never goes HIGH. How long does pulseIn() wait by default, what does it return when it gives up, and what does the robot do with that number?

Show solution
  1. No timeout. With no pulse arriving, pulseIn() waits for its default timeout of one second, and the whole loop freezes with it. Pass a timeout: pulseIn(ECHO, HIGH, 30000UL).
  2. Timeouts become 0 cm. pulseIn() returns 0 when it gives up, and this function turns that into "0 cm away", so after each freeze the robot brakes for an obstacle that isn't there. Return a sentinel instead:

The LOW pulse first makes sure TRIG starts from a clean low level, and unsigned long matches what pulseIn() actually returns.

#Exercise 6: Notice when the robot is stuck

A robot pushing against a low step that the sensor can't see keeps "driving", but its distance reading doesn't change. Write a watchdog: if the reading hasn't moved by 2 cm or more in 3 seconds of DRIVING, report STUCK. Test it in Python on a moving log and a stuck log.

Need a hint?

Keep a reference reading and the time you took it. Whenever the distance has moved 2 cm or more from the reference, take a new reference. If the reference gets 3 seconds old, you're stuck.

Show solution

The Arduino version keeps the same two variables:

Notice the cm < 150. A robot cruising down a long, empty corridor also sees an unchanging distance (no echo, or the far wall), and without that condition it would declare itself stuck. Every watchdog needs a test for its false alarms, not just its alarms.

#Challenge: Replay tests for the state machine

Testing by dragging a slider is slow, and you can't repeat it exactly. Instead, port the obstacle-avoider's transition rules to Python, then replay recorded distance sequences through it and compare the states it visits with what you expected. Use one reading per 60 ms and these rules: DRIVING to BACKING_UP under 20 cm; BACKING_UP to TURNING after 400 ms; TURNING to DRIVING after 500 ms once the reading is over 35 cm. Write four scenarios: a wall ahead, a noisy wall hovering at 19 to 21 cm, sensor dropouts while driving, and a robot boxed in so the path never clears. One of them will fail. Add a rule that fixes it.

Need a hint?

Represent a run by the list of distinct states it passed through, such as ["DRIVING", "BACKING_UP", "TURNING", "DRIVING"]. The boxed-in robot turns forever under the original rules; what should it do instead?

Show solution

Without the in_state >= 3000 rule, "boxed in" fails: the robot ends in TURNING and would spin until the battery dies. Two other details earn their place. The 0 <= cm check makes dropouts (-1) harmless, which the "dropouts" scenario proves. And "noisy wall" checks that the robot never flips back to DRIVING while readings hover around 20 cm. On the Arduino, STUCK would stop the motors and flash an LED, waiting for a human.
