m8-l1.html:
What you'll learn

  • Choose a capstone robot that stretches you without stalling you.
  • Write a one-page plan: behavior, pin map, state diagram, safety features, and a first test list.
  • Estimate a real robot's average and peak current, and what each one decides.
  • Set five milestones that each end with something you can demonstrate.

The most common capstone disaster isn't a bug. It's discovering, two days before the deadline, that the servo and the left motor's speed pin both want pin 9, or that nobody decided what the robot does when its path never clears. Both are five-minute fixes on paper and two-day fixes in code.

So this lesson has no code to run on the robot. You'll leave with a plan, and the next lesson turns it into a build.

#What you'll hand in

Whichever robot you choose, the finished capstone has seven parts. They're the same seven things a robotics team presents at a design review:

  1. A working robot in Wokwi (a saved project link, or copies of sketch.ino and diagram.json), or optionally a real chassis.
  2. A circuit: the diagram, with every pin in your pin plan.
  3. Sensor logic: filtered readings, with "no echo" or "line lost" handled on purpose.
  4. Motor control through driver signals (ENA/IN1/IN2 and ENB/IN3/IN4), never straight from a pin to a motor.
  5. Explicit states: a state diagram, and code with one case per state.
  6. A safety checklist, with each item either done or explained.
  7. A test plan with results, and an iteration report: what failed, what you changed, and what happened next.

#Pick a project

All five ideas run entirely in Wokwi. The LEDs from module 5 stand in for the motor driver, and you play the world with the sensor sliders.

Idea Level What it does Wokwi parts The hard part
Bumper bot Starter Drives, backs up, and turns away when something is closer than 20 cm HC-SR04, 6 driver LEDs, button Hysteresis and minimum times so it never twitches
Scanning avoider Intermediate When blocked, stops, looks left and right with a servo, and turns toward the clearer side Add a servo under the sensor Waiting for the servo and the filter before trusting a reading
Line follower with recovery Intermediate Follows a dark line with P control; searches when it loses the line; gives up after 3 s Two photoresistor modules instead of the HC-SR04 Calibration and choosing the gain
Line follower with a stop zone Advanced Follows a line, and pauses (not crashes) when something blocks the track Both sensors Two behaviors that must never fight over the motors
Real chassis Any level, optional Any of the above on a two-wheel kit with an L298N or TB6612FNG Real parts Power, wiring, and a floor that isn't perfect

Pick the one where you can name the hard part but don't yet know how you'll solve it. If you're unsure, the scanning avoider is the best balance: it uses every module of this course.

#Fix the pin plan first

Every project in this course uses the same pin plan, chosen so the PWM pins survive the Servo library. Copy it, then cross out what your robot doesn't use:

Pin Job Why this pin
5 ENA, left motor speed PWM, unaffected by the Servo library
7, 8 IN1, IN2, left motor direction Any digital pin works
6 ENB, right motor speed PWM, unaffected by the Servo library
4, 3 IN3, IN4, right motor direction Any digital pin works
9 Scanning servo Servo signal can use any pin; 9 and 10 lose PWM anyway
10, 11 HC-SR04 TRIG, ECHO Plain digital I/O
2 Start/stop button to GND INPUT_PULLUP, pressed reads LOW
A0, A1 Left and right line sensors Analog inputs

#Draw the states before the code

Your state diagram is the contract between your plan and your code. Here's the scanning avoider's. Every arrow is a rule you'll write as an if, and every bubble becomes a case:

Two things to check in your own diagram. Every state needs a way out (or a good reason to be final, like a stuck robot waiting for a human). And the robot must power up in a state where the motors are off: WAITING here.

#Fill in the planning template

Copy this into a document and fill in every line. Short answers are fine; blank ones are not.

#If you build it for real: the power check

Skip this section if you're staying in Wokwi. For a real robot, two currents matter, and they answer different questions. Peak current (both wheels stalled) decides whether the driver and wiring can cope. Average current decides how long the battery lasts. Here's an estimate for the scanning avoider on 4 × AA NiMH cells, using Adafruit's TT motor figures and assumed values for the rest:

Over four hours of running is plenty for testing. The 2.7 A peak is why the motors get their own pack and why stall situations need a watchdog in code.

#The safety checklist

Every item applies in Wokwi too, because the habit is the point. In your report, mark each one done or explain why it doesn't apply.

# Safety item How you show it
S1 Motors are off at power-up: drive(0, 0) runs first in setup(), and the robot starts in WAITING Code and log
S2 A button press stops the robot from any moving state, and it stays stopped until pressed again Test
S3 A top-speed limit in drive() that no other code can exceed Code
S4 No-echo readings and lost-line readings are handled on purpose, never as 0 cm Code and test
S5 A time limit on every state that waits for the world (turning, searching) Code and test
S6 Real robot: first run with wheels off the table Photo or note
S7 Real robot: separate motor battery, shared ground, no bare battery leads; AA cells, not loose lithium cells Photo

#Milestones

Each milestone ends with something you can demonstrate, so you're never more than one step from a working robot:

Before moving on, check your plan against these questions. Can you name the state your robot is in at every moment? Does every state have an exit? Which number are you least sure about, and which test will tell you? If you can answer all three, you're ready to build.

Key takeaways

  • Plan first: pin conflicts and missing transitions are cheap on paper and expensive in code.
  • Choose a project whose hard part you can name but haven't solved yet.
  • Draw the state diagram before writing a case, and make the power-up state safe.
  • Peak current sizes the driver and wiring; average current sets battery life.
  • Milestones that each end in a demo keep a working robot in your hands the whole time.

m8-l2.html:
What you'll learn

  • Set up the capstone circuit in Wokwi and read the starter sketch's structure.
  • Reach each milestone's demo before starting the next one.
  • Test decision logic in Python before writing it in C++.
  • Adapt the build for a line follower, or for a real chassis.

You won't start from a blank sketch. The starter below already drives two motors through driver signals, reads a filtered distance, stops on a button press, and logs everything, because you built each of those pieces in modules 5 to 7. What it doesn't have is behavior. Three states are marked TODO, and filling them in is the capstone.

#What we're building

The scanning avoider, the intermediate project from the last lesson. The other projects reuse most of this; the line-follower changes come at the end.

#Set up the circuit

New Arduino Uno project on wokwi.com (opens in a new tab). Replace diagram.json with the one below, then add the Servo library in the Library Manager tab. Six LEDs show the driver inputs, left motor on top and right motor below: EN is speed (brightness), and the two IN LEDs show direction.

#The starter sketch

Paste this into sketch.ino. Read it top to bottom once before changing anything; every function in it comes from an earlier module.

Run it, press START/STOP, and drag the HC-SR04 slider below 20 cm. The log shows the robot go from WAITING to DRIVING to BACKING_UP, and then sit there with the motors off, because BACKING_UP is still a TODO:

Notice the log keeps running during every state, and the button works in every state. That's the payoff of the non-blocking structure: you can add behavior without breaking either.

#Milestone 1: Wiring and motor self-test

Goal: prove every driver signal is on the pin the code thinks it is, before any behavior depends on it. Write selfTest() and call it at the end of setup(): each wheel forward then backward for 400 ms, one at a time, then the servo to 30°, 90°, and 150°.

Demo: the LEDs light in this order: L-EN with L-IN1, L-EN with L-IN2, R-EN with R-IN3, R-EN with R-IN4. Then the servo steps across. On a real robot, do this with the wheels in the air (safety S6).

Show solution

Using delay() is fine here. The self-test runs once, before the robot is allowed to drive, and it's meant to be watched. If the wrong LED lights, fix the wiring or the pin constants now; every later milestone assumes this one passed.

#Milestone 2: Sensor, filter, and log

Goal: confirm the sensor pipeline works in this circuit. The starter already pings every 60 ms, rounds, and filters with a median of five.

Demo: in WAITING, set the slider to 30, 100, and 250 cm; the cm column should be within a centimeter or so of each. Then jump from 100 to 15 and count log lines: cm should follow within about three samples. If you want to test fault handling here too, paste injectFault() and the slide switch from the module 7 harness into this sketch.

#Milestone 3: The core states

Goal: fill in BACKING_UP and TURNING so the robot backs up for 400 ms, then spins left until the path is clear beyond 35 cm, with at least 400 ms of turning (no twitching) and at most 3 seconds (safety S5).

Demo: with the slider below 20 cm, the log shows DRIVING, BACKING_UP, TURNING. Raise the slider above 35 cm during the turn and it returns to DRIVING. Leave the slider low and after 3 seconds it gives up and goes to WAITING.

Need a hint?

BACKING_UP only needs a drive command and one timed exit. TURNING has two exits: the clear-path one (time and distance) and the time limit. Decide what a reading of -1 (no echo at all) should mean when you're checking for a clear path.

Show solution

A filtered -1 means no echo for five pings in a row, which in open space means "nothing in range", so it counts as clear here. The minimum 400 ms is the hysteresis in time; the 35 cm exit versus the 20 cm entry is the hysteresis in distance.

#Milestone 4: Look before you turn

Goal: after backing up, stop, point the servo left and take a reading, point it right and take another, face forward, then turn toward the side with more room.

There's a Wokwi catch. The simulated sensor doesn't know where the servo points; the slider sets one distance for every direction. So you play the room: while the servo looks left, set the slider to the left-hand distance, then change it while the servo looks right. To give your hand time, each look lasts LOOK_MS. Use 2000 ms in Wokwi; about 500 ms is plenty on a real robot (enough for the servo to arrive and the median to refill).

Write the decision rule in Python first and test the awkward cases, including a side with no echo and a tie:

Need a hint?

SCANNING has three phases: look left, look right, face forward. Keep the phase in a global int scanPhase, reset it to 0 when BACKING_UP hands over, and record each reading at the end of its phase, when the filter has had time to refill.

Show solution

New globals near the top:

The three states that change:

The servo faces forward before TURNING starts, so the turn ends on what's ahead, not on what was to the side. If your servo is mounted the other way round, the robot will turn toward the closer side; swap 150 and 30.

#Milestone 5: Safety features

Goal: finish the safety checklist. The starter already covers S1 (motors off first), S2 (button stops anything), and S3 (MAX_SPEED). Add:

  1. A start delay. After START, wait one second before the wheels turn, so a hand can get clear.
  2. A stuck watchdog in DRIVING, from module 7: if the distance hasn't changed by 2 cm in 3 seconds while something is within 150 cm, log STUCK and go to WAITING.
Show solution

Two globals, set every time DRIVING begins (add the if to the end of enterState()):

The new DRIVING case:

In Wokwi the robot never really moves, so if you leave the slider under 150 cm during DRIVING, the watchdog fires after 3 seconds. That isn't a false alarm; it's the watchdog correctly noticing a robot that isn't getting anywhere. Drag the slider slowly toward the robot to simulate driving, and it stays quiet.

#Variant: the line follower

For a line-follower project, swap the HC-SR04 and servo for two photoresistor sensor modules: AO of the left one to A0, the right one to A1, VCC to 5V, GND to GND. Each module has a light slider; with this module, less light means a higher reading, so set a sensor to about 10 lux for "over the dark line" and leave it at 500 lux for "white floor".

The state list becomes WAITING, CALIBRATING, FOLLOWING, SEARCHING. Calibration and following look like this; SEARCHING is the one from the module 6 challenge:

The braces after case CALIBRATING: and case FOLLOWING: are required because those cases declare variables. In Wokwi you can't drive along a real line, so test the controller by setting the sliders: left dark and right light should push the right wheel faster than the left (the robot steers left, toward the line), and both light for 200 ms should start a search. For the advanced project, add the HC-SR04 back on pins 10 and 11 and a PAUSED state that FOLLOWING enters when something is within 20 cm.

#Moving to a real chassis

The sketch runs unchanged; only the wiring and a few numbers move:

  • Wire pins 5, 7, 8, 6, 4, 3 to ENA, IN1, IN2, ENB, IN3, IN4 on the driver (remove the ENA and ENB jumpers on an L298N). Motor pack to the driver's motor supply, grounds joined.
  • Mount the HC-SR04 level, about 10 cm above the floor, clear of the wheels. Set LOOK_MS to about 500.
  • Run milestone 1 with the wheels in the air, then lower CRUISE until the robot can stop within STOP_CM at full speed. The filter delay from module 7 means a fast robot needs a larger stop distance.
  • Expect to retune every number. That's what the next lesson's test plan is for.

Key takeaways

  • Start from a skeleton whose infrastructure works, and add behavior one milestone at a time.
  • Each milestone ends with a demo you can check in the log.
  • Test decision rules in Python, including the awkward cases, before writing them in C++.
  • In Wokwi you play the world: the slider is every wall, and it only moves when you do.
  • Safety features (start delay, button stop, time limits, watchdog) are part of the build, not extras.

m8-l3.html:
What you'll learn

  • Run a full test plan in Wokwi (or on a chassis) and record evidence for every result.
  • Write an iteration report that links each change to a failed test and a re-run.
  • Present the robot in two minutes: behavior, states, evidence, and what's next.
  • Assess the project against the rubric, and choose a next step after the course.

"It works" is not a result. "It passed 10 of 10 tests, here are the log lines, and here's the regression we found and fixed on the way" is a result, and it's what separates a robotics project from a robot that happened to work once. This lesson turns your build into that kind of evidence.

#Step 1: Run the test plan

Here's a plan for the scanning avoider, written so every test can be run in Wokwi by moving the distance slider and pressing the button. Copy it, add rows for anything your robot does differently, and fill in the last column as you go. Line followers can start from the plan in the module 7 practice.

ID What you do Pass if the log shows Result
T1 Start the simulation; don't press anything for 5 s Only WAITING, with left and right at 0
T2 Press START; after 2 s, drag slowly from 150 to 15 cm BACKING_UP begins before cm drops below 15, then SCANNING
T3 In DRIVING, wiggle the slider between 19 and 22 for 5 s No transition less than 400 ms after the previous one
T4 During the scan: 120 cm while it looks left, 40 while it looks right scan: left 120 cm, right 40 (give or take a centimeter), then a left turn: L-IN2 and R-IN3 lit
T5 Same, but 40 left and 120 right A right turn: L-IN1 and R-IN4 lit
T6 Keep the slider at 15 through the scan and turn TURNING lasts 3 s, then WAITING
T7 Once TURNING starts, slide to 100 DRIVING again, no sooner than 400 ms into the turn
T8 Press the button during TURNING WAITING on the very next log line, motors at 0
T9 Press START and watch the first second Motors stay at 0 for 1 s, then 160
T10 In DRIVING, leave the slider at 80 for 4 s; repeat at 300 STUCK at 80 cm; no STUCK at 300 cm

To record evidence, select the relevant lines in the Serial Monitor, copy them, and paste them under the test in your report. A test without a log excerpt counts as "not run".

💡 Tip

Run the plan from the top after every change, not just the test you were fixing. That full re-run is the regression test, and it's the only way to catch a fix that breaks something else.

#Step 2: Write the iteration report

Each time a test fails and you change something, write one entry. Keep it short, and keep it honest: a failure you explain well is worth more than one you hide.

That's an example entry for a real chassis, and it shows why the full re-run matters: the fix for T2 broke T11, and a single-test check would never have shown it. Iteration 3 then fixes the cause (too much speed near obstacles) instead of the symptom.

A summary chart makes the story visible at a glance. Record each test's result per iteration, and let Python find the fixes and the regressions:

The bar chart alone says iterations 1 and 2 were equally good. The printout says iteration 2 fixed one test and broke another, which is the real story. Put both in your report.

#Step 3: Present it in two minutes

A short screen recording of Wokwi (or a phone video of the chassis) with the Serial Monitor visible is the best format. Your computer has a recorder built in: Shift-Command-5 on a Mac, the Snipping Tool's record mode on Windows 11, and Screen capture on a Chromebook. Follow this outline:

Time Show Say
0:00 to 0:15 The robot running What it does, in one sentence
0:15 to 0:45 Your state diagram The states, and the one transition you're proudest of
0:45 to 1:30 A live run with the log scrolling One normal run, then one tricky test (T6 or T8 are good)
1:30 to 2:00 Your iteration chart One failure, what you changed, and what you'd do next

To share the simulation, use Wokwi's Save and then Share to get a link, the same way you saved projects in module 1. Before sharing, check that the project's name and description contain nothing personal.

#Step 4: The rubric

Score yourself honestly before you submit; then compare with your teacher's or a classmate's score. Each row is worth up to 4 points, for a total of 28.

Criterion 1: Beginning 2: Developing 3: Proficient 4: Excellent
Circuit and pin plan Circuit incomplete or pins conflict Works, but no pin plan Pin plan matches circuit; no conflicts Plus clear labels, and real-hardware wiring notes
Sensor handling Raw readings used directly Filtered, but no-echo or lost-line becomes 0 Filtered, with bad data handled on purpose Plus calibration or fault-injection evidence
Motor control and safety Motor logic scattered through the code One drive function, but no speed limit or stop Driver signals through drive(), S1 to S5 done Plus ramping or proportional slow-down, all of S1 to S7 addressed
States and transitions No explicit states States exist but some have no exit Diagram matches code; every state has an exit Plus hysteresis and time limits that are justified by tests
Testing A few informal tries Tests listed but no pass criteria 10 or more tests with criteria and log evidence Plus edge cases and full re-runs after each change
Iteration report No record of changes Changes listed without evidence Each change linked to a failed test and a re-run Plus a regression found and explained
Communication Hard to follow Covers the behavior only Behavior, states, evidence in about two minutes Plus a clear "what I'd do next" grounded in results

#Where to go next

Your robot uses the same loop as far bigger machines: sense, decide with explicit states, act, measure, adjust. Some directions from here:

  • Close the loop on speed. Add wheel encoders and use the I and D terms of PID control, so the robot drives straight even when one motor is weaker.
  • Go wireless. Wokwi also simulates the ESP32, which has Wi-Fi and Bluetooth, so the same robot logic can report its log to a web page.
  • Build the real one. A two-wheel chassis kit, an L298N or TB6612FNG, and 4 × AA cells is enough to run your capstone sketch unchanged except for the numbers.
  • Join a team. FIRST, VEX, World Robot Olympiad, and RoboCup Junior all run student robotics competitions, and every one of them rewards the test-and-iterate habits you used here.

Key takeaways

  • A result is a test with a pass criterion and log evidence, not "it worked when I tried it".
  • Re-run the whole plan after every change; regressions are only visible that way.
  • An iteration report links a failed test, a hypothesis, one change, and a re-run.
  • Present the behavior, the states, the evidence, and the next step, in about two minutes.
